section: Set random seed and the device for predicting from the model
text:
Set random seed and the device for predicting from the model
If you have a GPU, this is where it will be specified (automatically).


Show code
# Reproducibility — fix random seeds so results are the same on every run.
# Prediction is not deterministic: simulate_trajectory() samples a next location
# from the predicted probability surface at every step, so without a seed two
# runs of the same trained model give different trajectories (and a different
# heatmap).  Seeding here makes a set of simulations reproducible.
torch.manual_seed(42)
np.random.seed(42)

# DEVICE is capitalised — module-level constant (set once, never reassigned).
# get_device() returns 'cuda' if a GPU is available, 'mps' on Apple Silicon,
# or 'cpu' otherwise.  All tensors and the model are moved to this device.
DEVICE = deepssf.get_device()
print(f"Device: {DEVICE}")


Device: mps

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
Set script paths
These must point at the same data and rasters the model was trained on — the model takes one input channel per raster band, in LAYER_PATHS order, so a different set of layers (or a different order) either fails to load the weights or feeds the wrong covariate into each filter.
OUTPUT_DIR is the directory a training run wrote its checkpoints to, given here as a literal path rather than through get_output_dir() (which mints a new dated directory). Figures and rasters produced below are written back into the same directory, alongside the model they came from.
All-caps names below are module-level constants — set once here and referenced throughout the notebook without being reassigned. Python has no built-in constant keyword, so capitalisation is the community convention (PEP 8) to signal “do not change this value”.


Show code
DATA_DIR = Path("data")  # location of the bundled sample data
MAPPING_DIR = Path("mapping")  # location of the landcover mapping files
CSV_PATH = DATA_DIR / "pigs_east_alligator_steps_covs_20261015.csv"  # GPS tracking data, 28 individuals

# NOTE: 's2' and 's2_dir' are RESERVED keys in load_environmental_layers().
# 's2_dir' triggers the monthly-composite loader (load_s2_data), and a plain
# 's2' entry is skipped by the per-file loop — so a single multi-band GeoTIFF
# must be given any *other* name, otherwise nothing is loaded and the function
# raises "raster_transform could not be set".
LAYER_PATHS = {
    # Topographic layers (DEM, slope)
    "dem": str(MAPPING_DIR / "DEM_east_alligator_3112.tif"),
    "slope": str(MAPPING_DIR / "slope_east_alligator_3112.tif"),
    "water": str(MAPPING_DIR / "water_east_alligator.tif"),

    # AlphaEarth embeddings (2025)
    "alphaearth": str(MAPPING_DIR / "alphaearth_2025_east_alligator_3112.tif"),
}

# The training run to predict from — where its checkpoints were written by
# deepssf_piggies_train.ipynb, and where the outputs below are saved.
OUTPUT_DIR = Path("outputs/alphaearth/2026-10-29_1")
CKPT_PATH = OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model.pt"

if not CKPT_PATH.exists():
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"No checkpoint at {CKPT_PATH} — set OUTPUT_DIR to a directory that "
        "deepssf_piggies_train.ipynb has finished writing to."
    )
print(f"Output directory: {OUTPUT_DIR}")
print("Checkpoints:", ", ".join(sorted(p.name for p in OUTPUT_DIR.glob("*.pt"))))


Output directory: outputs/alphaearth/2026-10-29_1
Checkpoints: best_model.pt, best_model_habitat.pt, best_model_movement.pt

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
load_environmental_layers()
Reads each GeoTIFF listed in LAYER_PATHS, min–max

Scales every band to [0, 1], and returns:

env_layers — dict mapping layer name → NumPy array: 2-D (H × W) for single-band GeoTIFFs, 3-D (bands × H × W) for multi-band ones, where each band becomes its own model input channel
raster_transform — Affine object that converts pixel (row, col) indices to the projected coordinates (easting, northing) of the raster(s), which should be in the same CRS as the GPS data. This transform is used whenever we need to translate between pixel space and real-world coordinates.


Two things to watch for:

The keys 's2' and 's2_dir' are reserved for the monthly Sentinel-2 composite loader — a single GeoTIFF passed under the name 's2' is silently skipped (see the note in the paths cell above).
The rescaling uses a single global min/max across all bands of a file, and computes (data - lo) / hi rather than (data - lo) / (hi - lo). Our index raster is int16 scaled by 10 000 with ±10 000 fill values, so the loaded values span [0, 2] rather than [0, 1] and the three indices are not individually normalised. That is workable (the CNN can rescale internally) but if it hurts training, pre-scale each band yourself and save as .npy — non-.tif paths in LAYER_PATHS are loaded with np.load(..., mmap_mode='r') and left untouched, though at least one real .tif must remain in the dict so the transform can be set.



Show code
env_layers, raster_transform = deepssf.load_environmental_layers(LAYER_PATHS)
print("Layers loaded:", list(env_layers.keys()))
for name, arr in env_layers.items():
    print(f"  {name}: shape={arr.shape}, min={arr.min():.3f}, max={arr.max():.3f}")

# Each band of a multi-band layer becomes one CNN input channel, so count bands
# (not layers) here and reuse the total when setting ModelParams below.  Deriving
# it means switching rasters in LAYER_PATHS needs no other edits.
N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS = sum(1 if arr.ndim == 2 else arr.shape[0] for arr in env_layers.values())
print(f"Spatial channels: {N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS}")

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
prepare_movement_df()
Converts a fixes dataframe (one row per GPS location) into a step dataframe (one row per movement between consecutive fixes).

For each step it computes:

dx, dy — displacement in projected CRS units (metres)
bearing — direction of travel (radians; 0 = north, clockwise positive)
bearing_tm1 — bearing of the previous step, used as a model input so the network can capture directional persistence by estimating a turning angle
dt_hour — time elapsed between consecutive fixes (hours)
hour_t1, yday_t1 — decimal hour-of-day and day-of-year at the step start location
*_sin1 / *_cos1 — sine/cosine encodings of hour and yday (see SCALAR_COLS below)


The trailing underscore on column names (x1_, y1_, t1_, etc.) flags them as “start of step” variables; x2_, y2_, t2_ are the corresponding “end of step” values, following the convention of the amt package (Signer et al. 2019). The last fix for each individual is dropped because no forward step can be formed.


Show code
# The CSV is already in amt step format, but prepare_movement_df() expects one row
# per *fix* and rebuilds the steps itself (it also derives bearing, dt_hour and the
# cyclic time encodings the model needs).  Point it at the step-start columns and
# let it re-form the steps from consecutive fixes.
step_df = deepssf.prepare_movement_df(
    raw_df, 
    id_col="name", 
    time_col="t1_", 
    x_col="x1_", 
    y_col="y1_"
)
n_dropped = len(raw_df) - len(step_df)
print(f"Movement steps : {len(step_df):,}  ({n_dropped} dropped — last per individual)")
step_df.head()

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
SCALAR_COLS
These are non-spatial inputs. For processing with convolutional layers, they are converted into spatial windows (rasters/arrays), and stacked with the truly spatial covariates.
The model receives a fixed-size spatial window centred on each step’s start location. To let the network express time-varying habitat preferences (e.g. different nocturnal vs diurnal use), scalar covariates are tiled into additional channels of the same H × W size, so every pixel “knows” the current time context when habitat suitability is estimated.

hour_t1_sin1 / hour_t1_cos1

Sine and cosine of (2π × hour / 24), encoding time-of-day as a circular variable. The circular encoding means 23:00 and 01:00 are treated as adjacent — a plain hour value would have an artificial discontinuity at midnight.

yday_t1_sin1 / yday_t1_cos1

Same circular encoding for day-of-year (1–365), capturing seasonal variation in habitat use (e.g. dry-season vs wet-season movements).

dt_hour

Elapsed time between consecutive fixes (hours). Because GPS collars do not always fix at a perfectly regular rate, including dt_hour lets the movement kernel rescale expected displacement proportionally to the actual time interval rather than assuming a fixed fix rate. Note: dt_hour must be supplied at simulation time as well, so that simulate_trajectory() produces inputs consistent with training.




Show code
SCALAR_COLS = ["hour_t1_sin1",
               "hour_t1_cos1", 
               "yday_t1_sin1", 
               "yday_t1_cos1", 
               "dt_hour"]

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
WINDOW_SIZE
The size of the local availability window in cells/pixels - should match what was in the training script.


Show code
WINDOW_SIZE = 51

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
PIXEL_SIZE
Raster resolution in CRS units (metres here). Read straight off raster_transform rather than typed in: the transform is the authority on the grid the model is trained against, and a hand-entered value that disagrees with it silently mis-scales the movement kernel — which is parameterised in metres — against a grid measured in pixels.


Show code
# transform.a is the cell width, transform.e the (negative) cell height
PIXEL_SIZE = abs(raster_transform.a)

if not math.isclose(abs(raster_transform.a), abs(raster_transform.e)):
    raise ValueError(
        f"Non-square pixels ({abs(raster_transform.a)} x {abs(raster_transform.e)}); "
        "the model assumes square cells."
    )
print(f"Pixel size: {PIXEL_SIZE} m  →  window {WINDOW_SIZE} px = "
      f"{WINDOW_SIZE * PIXEL_SIZE:,.0f} m across")


Pixel size: 20.0 m  →  window 51 px = 1,020 m across

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
filter_steps_by_window()
Removes steps whose straight-line displacement exceeds half the spatial window (WINDOW_SIZE × PIXEL_SIZE / 2 metres). Such steps would place the true next location outside the predicted probability map, causing an index error in the loss function.


Show code
step_df = deepssf.filter_steps_by_window(
    step_df, window_size=WINDOW_SIZE, pixel_size=PIXEL_SIZE
)
print(f"Steps after window filter: {len(step_df):,}")


Steps after window filter: 249,584

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
params_from_checkpoint()
Weights only load into a model built with the same architecture, so predicting from a trained model means reproducing its hyper-parameters exactly. Rather than re-typing the training notebook’s constants here — where a habitat branch one layer too shallow fails loudly, but a mis-set pixel_size quietly rescales the movement kernel — params_from_checkpoint() recovers them from the checkpoint and returns the ModelParams to hand to ConvJointModel.
deepssf writes the ModelParams dict into every checkpoint, so for a model trained with 0.3.1 or later it is simply read back. Older checkpoints (anything in outputs/ trained before then) do not have it, and the architecture is recovered from the layer shapes instead: a conv weight is [out_channels, in_channels, k, k] and a linear weight [out_features, in_features], which between them pin down every hyper-parameter that changes a tensor shape — input_channels, output_channels, kernel_size, both conv-layer counts, dense_dim_in_all, dense_dim_hidden and num_movement_params. Either way the result is checked against the saved tensors, so a stored params dict that contradicts its own weights raises here rather than failing later inside load_state_dict.
Three things it cannot get from the file, passed in below:

image_dim — the habitat branch is fully convolutional, so nothing in the weights records the training window. The movement branch’s flattened size does constrain it, and that is checked, but only to within the slack that max-pooling’s floor division allows (48–55 px all flatten to the same 288 here). WINDOW_SIZE also has to match filter_steps_by_window() above, and is the window the simulations step within.
pixel_size — a property of the raster, read off raster_transform.
device — where the model is being run, which has nothing to do with where it was trained; it defaults to this machine rather than to the recorded value.

n_scalar_covariates only fills the two ModelParams fields that no layer reads; the scalar count that matters is folded into input_channels, which comes off the weights. The check below is the one thing the checkpoint cannot do for us — that the covariates loaded in this notebook are the ones the model was trained on. It compares counts only, so keep LAYER_PATHS in the training run’s order.


Show code
params = deepssf.params_from_checkpoint(
    str(CKPT_PATH),
    image_dim=WINDOW_SIZE,               # not recorded in the weights
    pixel_size=PIXEL_SIZE,               # from raster_transform
    n_scalar_covariates=len(SCALAR_COLS),
    device=DEVICE,                       # this machine, not the training machine
)
for name, value in params.to_dict().items():
    print(f"  {name:26s}: {value}")

# The covariates in this notebook must be the ones the model was trained on.
# input_channels is one channel per raster band plus one per scalar covariate,
# so a changed LAYER_PATHS or SCALAR_COLS shows up here as a count mismatch.
n_expected = N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS + len(SCALAR_COLS)
if n_expected != params.input_channels:
    raise ValueError(
        f"{N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS} raster bands + {len(SCALAR_COLS)} scalars = {n_expected} "
        f"input channels, but the checkpoint was trained with {params.input_channels}. "
        "LAYER_PATHS or SCALAR_COLS differ from the training run."
    )
print(f"\n{N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS} raster bands + {len(SCALAR_COLS)} scalars = "
      f"{params.input_channels} input channels - matches the checkpoint")

  image_dim                 : 51
  pixel_size                : 20.0
  dim_in_nonspatial_to_grid : 5
  dense_dim_in_nonspatial   : 5
  dense_dim_hidden          : 128
  dense_dim_in_all          : 72

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
ConvJointModel
The deepSSF model! A joint habitat–movement model with two heads: 1. Habitat head — a small CNN applied to the spatial window (env layers + tiled scalars) that outputs a per-pixel log-suitability map. 2. Movement head — a dense MLP (fully-connected layer) that takes the scalar covariates and the previous bearing, and produces parameters for a parametric movement kernel (a mixture of wrapped distributions centred on the current location).
The two log-probability surfaces are summed pixel-wise to give the joint predicted probability map for the animal’s next step.


Show code
model = deepssf.ConvJointModel(params).to(DEVICE)
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Model parameters : {n_params:,}")


Model parameters : 43,117

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
Load the trained model
ConvJointModel above is freshly initialised — random weights — so nothing it predicts means anything until a checkpoint is loaded into it. A training run writes three:

best_model.pt — the model to use for simulation. Both heads from one epoch, so the joint likelihood is the one that was actually measured.
best_model_habitat.pt / best_model_movement.pt — each head at its own best epoch, tracked across the whole run.

Mixing them is a deliberate trade: taking the habitat head from a different epoch gives the sharpest habitat surface to map, but the two heads then come from different epochs and the joint model’s likelihood is no longer what either checkpoint recorded. Use it for the landscape predictions below, not for simulating trajectories.
load_checkpoint() loads the weights in place and is strict about shapes, so a mismatch between the constants set above and the trained architecture raises here rather than silently predicting from a partly-random model.


Show code
# The joint model — what the simulations further down should use
ckpt = deepssf.load_checkpoint(str(CKPT_PATH), model)
print(f"best_model.pt          saved on '{ckpt['checkpoint_criterion']}' "
      f"= {ckpt['checkpoint_score']:.6f}")
print(f"                       trained with deepssf {ckpt.get('deepssf_version', 'unknown')}, "
      f"val_loss {ckpt['val_loss']:.6f}")

hab_ckpt = deepssf.load_checkpoint(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_habitat.pt"))
print(f"best_model_habitat.pt  saved on '{hab_ckpt['checkpoint_criterion']}' "
      f"= {hab_ckpt['checkpoint_score']:.6f}")
print(f"(a uniform surface over the window scores {np.log(WINDOW_SIZE ** 2):.4f})")

# Prediction only — no gradients needed, and this turns off dropout/batchnorm
# training behaviour.
model.eval()

# To map the sharpest habitat surface instead, overwrite just that head:
# load_head_weights(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_habitat.pt"), model, "habitat")

                       trained with deepssf 0.3.1, val_loss 3.984106

title: deepSSF Predictions
section: Convert the NumPy rasters loaded earlier into PyTorch tensors
text:
Convert the NumPy rasters loaded earlier into PyTorch tensors
predict_habitat_landscape(), simulate_trajectory() and simulate_trajectories() all call get_landscape(month_index) to fetch the current environmental layers as a list of 2-D tensors.
With static (non-seasonal) rasters the month_index argument is unused. For seasonal data (e.g. monthly NDVI composites) you would index into a stack of layers here based on the current month.


Show code
# The simulation and prediction functions stack the list returned by
# get_landscape() along a new channel dimension, so every element must be a *2-D*
# tensor.  Unbind the band dimension of any multi-band layer so the channel order
# matches what MovementDataset fed the model during training.
landscape_tensors = []
for arr in env_layers.values():
    t = torch.from_numpy(np.asarray(arr).astype(np.float32))
    landscape_tensors.extend([t] if t.ndim == 2 else list(t))

print(f"Landscape channels: {len(landscape_tensors)}  (each {tuple(landscape_tensors[0].shape)})")


def get_landscape(_month_index):
    # Returns one 2-D tensor per spatial channel, in the same order as LAYER_PATHS.
    return landscape_tensors


Landscape channels: 67  (each (1335, 1715))

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
make_simulation_inputs
This function creates the sin/cos encodings for specific days and hours of the year, and is used when simulating to convert from days of the year and hours into sin/cos encodings. It will return a tuple of length n_steps.
Here, we just want the sin/cos encodings for a single point in time, so we just set n_steps to 1 and input a day of the year (PRED_YDAY, integer) and fractional hour (PRED_HOUR, float).


Show code
# Predict for one moment in time: 9:30 am on day 200.

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
predict_habitat_landscape()
Everything so far has run the model on a WINDOW_SIZE crop centred on the animal. But the habitat sub-network is fully convolutional — four 3x3 convolutions with stride 1 and padding 1, no pooling and no dense layer — so the same trained filters can be swept across the entire raster in a single pass. Convolution is translation-equivariant, so the value at a pixel is exactly what the model would have produced for a window centred on that pixel.
That gives a landscape-wide habitat selection surface. Read it as a relative ranking of cells: “if the animal were somewhere on this landscape, how attractive is each cell”. It deliberately says nothing about whether the animal could reach a cell in one step — that constraint lives in the movement kernel, which takes no part here. The two are only combined over a local window, which is what simulate_next_step() does.

Inputs:

model

the trained model; only model.conv_habitat is used

landscape_rasters

the spatial covariates as a list of 2-D tensors, in the same order and on the same scaling as training — i.e. exactly what get_landscape() returns

scalars

the scalar covariates for the moment being predicted, in SCALAR_COLS order. make_simulation_inputs() builds this row for us, so the encoding cannot drift from what the simulation uses. Each value is broadcast to a constant layer covering the whole landscape (the same thing Scalar_to_Grid_Block does for a window — that block can’t be reused here because its output size is fixed to WINDOW_SIZE)

normalise

subtract the log-sum-exp over the whole landscape, making the surface a log-probability that sums to 1 across all valid cells

edge_buffer

how many border pixels to mask as NaN. Defaults to habitat_edge_buffer(model) — the exact width the zero-padding reaches, 1 pixel per conv layer, so 4 here. Those pixels saw padding rather than landscape and are not comparable with the interior

chunk_rows

process this many raster rows at a time. A full-landscape activation is several hundred MB, enough to exhaust a GPU; the chunks overlap by edge_buffer so the result is identical to a single pass


Outputs: a [height, width] NumPy array of log-probabilities, NaN in the border. Take np.exp() for probabilities.



Show code

    model,
    landscape_rasters=get_landscape(0),   # static layers → month index 0
    scalars=scalars_pred,
)

print(f"probabilities sum to  : {np.nansum(np.exp(habitat_log)):.4f}")

How does habitat selection change through the day?
The scalar covariates are inputs to the habitat CNN, so the same landscape produces a different surface at different times of day. Re-running the prediction at different times of day shows what the model has learned.
Each surface is normalised over the landscape independently, so the panels show where selection is concentrated at that hour, not the overall level of activity.
These surfaces only show the habitat selection, and not where would expect to find pigs, as these maps do not take movement into consideration. To generate distribution maps we need to simulate movement trajectories.

    )

    ax.set_ylabel("Northing (m)")

Save the hourly habitat selection surfaces as a raster (TIF)
Writing them out with the raster’s transform and CRS means they can be opened directly in QGIS/ArcGIS or read back with rasterio, and overlaid on the other layers in mapping/.
One band per hour rather than one file per hour: the 24 surfaces share a grid, a transform and a CRS, so a single stack keeps them together and lets GIS software step through the day with the band slider. Band n is hour n - 1 (GDAL numbers bands from 1), and each band carries its hour in both its description and its tags — so src.read(15) is 14:00.

    driver="GTiff",

    width=width,
    count=len(hours_sorted),      # one band per hour
    dtype="float32",
    crs=raster_crs,
    transform=raster_transform,
    nodata=np.nan,          # the masked edge buffer
    compress="deflate",

        dst.set_band_description(band, f"habitat selection log prob {hour:02d}:00")

    dst.update_tags(prediction_yday=PRED_YDAY, hours=",".join(str(h) for h in hours_sorted))

text:
simulate_trajectory()
Generates a sequence of steps by iteratively: 1. Extracting a spatial window centred on the current location. 2. Running the model to obtain a joint log-probability surface over that window. 3. Sampling the next pixel from that surface (softmax-normalised probabilities). 4. Converting the sampled pixel back to projected coordinates and advancing time.

Inputs:

model

the trained model

get_landscape

retrieves the landscape layers (spatial covariates) that were used to train the model

transform

raster Affine transform

start_x

x coordinate of starting location

start_y

y coordinate of starting location

n_steps

number of steps

starting_yday

starting day-of-year

starting_hour

starting hour-of-day

time_between_steps

time between steps in hours

window_size

size in pixels of the local landscape

month_index_fn

a function mapping day-of-year → month index (used by the get_landscape function). Here we are using static spatial layers so we can set it to 0.


Outputs: DataFrame with one row per simulated step containing:

x, y
— projected coordinates of the simulated location
hour, yday
— time variables updated at each step
month_index

the month index used to index the spatial variables (will be 0 if using static spatial covariates)

text:
plot_trajectories_folium()
A static figure is fine for checking the overall shape of a trajectory, but not for asking where the animal actually went. This draws the simulated (and optionally observed) locations over a satellite basemap so you can zoom in on individual steps.

Inputs:

trajectories

a simulated-locations DataFrame. If it has a trajectory_id column (as simulate_trajectories() returns) each id is drawn as its own toggleable line; a plain sim_df is drawn as a single line.

observed

observed locations to overlay, e.g. step_df. Drawn as points rather than a line by default, because step_df holds 28 individuals and a single line would connect them with jumps that never happened.

src_crs

CRS of the input coordinates. Everything is reprojected to EPSG:4326 (lat/lon) for the web map — our data is in EPSG:3112.

basemap

"esri_imagery" (default), "esri_topo", "openstreetmap", or any XYZ tile-URL template. See the folium docs for more: https://python-visualization.github.io/folium/latest/user_guide/raster_layers/tiles.html

max_observed_points

observed locations are thinned to this many points. folium renders every point as its own element in the page, so all 100k+ fixes would lock up the notebook.

save_path

optionally also write a standalone HTML file.


Outputs: a folium.Map — leave it as the last line of a cell to display it.

folium is an optional dependency: pip install folium (or pip install "deepSSF[maps]").

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
simulate_trajectories()
Runs n_trajectories simulations and returns them stacked in one long-format DataFrame with trajectory_id and step columns.
Three methods are available:








method
how it works
when to use it




"batched" (default)
every trajectory takes its step together, so the model sees a batch of n_trajectories windows per forward pass instead of one
almost always — the forward pass is the whole cost of the simulation, and it is far better used at batch size 50 than at batch size 1


"sequential"
a plain loop over simulate_trajectory()
reference behaviour; needed if trajectories start at different times


"parallel"
the same loop across a thread pool
when start times vary and you want some overlap; the speed-up is modest (PyTorch releases the GIL inside its ops, but torch is already using several threads per op) and results are not reproducible from a seed



The one restriction on "batched" is that all trajectories share a clock, so starting_yday / starting_hour must be scalars. Start locations can still differ per trajectory — pass a list to start_x / start_y to release simulated animals from different points.

Get start points that are distributed across the prediction extent
We weight the starting points by the habitat selection probability at the time and yday of the first observed location.
We will discard locations from the start of the simulations so there isn’t too much of a bias towards these starting locations.


Show code
N_TRAJECTORIES = 2500   # how many simulated trajectories (one starting location each)

# Habitat selection surface at the time the simulations start (the first observed
# location), so starting locations are drawn where the model expects pigs to be
scalars_start = deepssf.make_simulation_inputs(
    n_steps=1, starting_yday=START_YDAY, starting_hour=START_HOUR
)[0][0]
start_surface = deepssf.predict_habitat_landscape(
    model, landscape_rasters=get_landscape(0), scalars=scalars_start
)

# Sampling weights: the surface is log-probability, so exponentiate.  NaN cells
# (the masked edge buffer, and wherever a covariate is missing) get zero weight,
# and renormalising guards against the surface not summing to exactly 1.
weights = np.nan_to_num(np.exp(start_surface.ravel()), nan=0.0)
weights /= weights.sum()

# With replacement, so N_TRAJECTORIES can exceed the number of cells.  A dedicated
# generator keeps the draw reproducible without depending on how many other numpy
# calls ran before this cell.
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
pick = rng.choice(weights.size, size=N_TRAJECTORIES, replace=True, p=weights)
rows, cols = np.unravel_index(pick, start_surface.shape)

# Cell centres → projected coordinates, then jitter within the cell so that
# trajectories drawn from the same cell don't share an exact starting point
start_xs, start_ys = rasterio.transform.xy(raster_transform, rows, cols)
start_xs = np.asarray(start_xs) + rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, N_TRAJECTORIES) * PIXEL_SIZE
start_ys = np.asarray(start_ys) + rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, N_TRAJECTORIES) * PIXEL_SIZE
print(f"{N_TRAJECTORIES:,} starting locations drawn from "
      f"{len(np.unique(pick)):,} distinct cells")

# Map the starting locations over the surface they were drawn from, with the same
# percentile colour limits as the habitat selection maps above
lo, hi = np.nanpercentile(start_surface, [COLOUR_PC_MIN, COLOUR_PC_MAX])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 6))
rasterio.plot.show(
    start_surface, transform=raster_transform, ax=ax,
    cmap="viridis", vmin=lo, vmax=hi,
)
ax.plot(start_xs, start_ys, "r.", markersize=1, alpha=0.5, label="starting locations")
ax.set_xlabel("Easting (m, projected)")
ax.set_ylabel("Northing (m, projected)")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", markerscale=8)
ax.set_title(f"{N_TRAJECTORIES:,} starting locations — habitat selection "
             f"(log prob), yday {START_YDAY:.0f}, {START_HOUR:.2f} h")
fig.colorbar(ax.images[0], ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label="log probability")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "random_starting_locations.png"), dpi=120)
plt.show()

section: Create a heatmap of the simulated trajectories
text:
Create a heatmap of the simulated trajectories
Count the number of simulated locations per cell/pixel, with an option to discard the first n steps to reduce bias towards the initial parameters.

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
trajectory_heatmap()

Inputs

trajectories

simulated locations, as returned by simulate_trajectories() (or a list of DataFrames).

transform, shape

the landscape rasters’ affine transform and (height, width), so the heatmap grid shares their origin and CRS.

burn_in

discard the first n steps of every trajectory. Early steps cluster around the release site(s) and reflect the starting conditions rather than the fitted model.

agg

aggregate agg x agg raster pixels into one heatmap cell. At the native 20 m almost every occupied cell holds a single location, so some coarsening makes the surface readable.


Outputs: (counts, heatmap_transform) — an int32 array of locations per cell, and its affine transform.

HEATMAP_PERIOD selects which part of the year the counts come from: "full" uses every simulated location, "wet" and "dry" keep only those whose day-of-year falls in the November–April wet season or the May–October dry season. The period is filtered before trajectory_heatmap() is called and named in the output filenames, so the three surfaces can be written side by side.
The result is visualised as a PNG below, written to a GeoTIFF with save_raster() so it can be opened in QGIS, and added to the interactive map as a layer that can be toggled on and off with add_heatmap_overlay().


Show code
HEATMAP_DF     = sim_many  # trajectories to summarise (or sim_many)
BURN_IN        = 1000              # drop the first n steps of every trajectory
HEATMAP_AGG    = 2              # heatmap cell = HEATMAP_AGG x HEATMAP_AGG raster pixels
HEATMAP_PERIOD = "full"         # "full", "wet" or "dry" — which part of the year to count

# Day-of-year bounds of the monsoonal seasons in the Top End: the wet runs
# November to April, the dry May to October.  The wet range wraps through New
# Year (305 > 120), which is why the filter below splits on start <= end.
SEASON_YDAYS = {
    "wet": (305, 120),   # 1 Nov - 30 Apr
    "dry": (121, 304),   # 1 May - 31 Oct
}

def filter_period(df, period):
    """Subset simulated locations to one season, using the simulated yday."""
    if period == "full":
        return df
    if period not in SEASON_YDAYS:
        raise ValueError(
            f"period must be 'full', 'wet' or 'dry', got {period!r}"
        )
    start, end = SEASON_YDAYS[period]
    # Floor to the calendar day: yday is fractional within a step (283.5 is
    # midday on day 283), and comparing the raw value would drop the steps
    # falling between the last day of one season and the first of the next.
    yday = np.floor(df["yday"])
    in_season = (
        yday.between(start, end) if start <= end else (yday >= start) | (yday <= end)
    )
    return df[in_season]


heatmap_df = filter_period(HEATMAP_DF, HEATMAP_PERIOD)
if heatmap_df.empty:
    raise ValueError(
        f"no simulated locations fall in the {HEATMAP_PERIOD} season — the "
        f"simulation spans yday {HEATMAP_DF['yday'].min():.0f} to "
        f"{HEATMAP_DF['yday'].max():.0f}"
    )

# Reused by the plot, GeoTIFF and web map below so they all describe the same
# subset: the number of trajectories that actually contribute locations, and a
# filename suffix naming the period.
N_HEATMAP_TRAJ = heatmap_df["trajectory_id"].nunique()
PERIOD_TAG = f"_{HEATMAP_PERIOD}"

heatmap, heatmap_transform = deepssf.trajectory_heatmap(
    heatmap_df,
    raster_transform,
    landscape_tensors[0].shape,
    burn_in=BURN_IN,
    agg=HEATMAP_AGG,
)

print(f"Period: {HEATMAP_PERIOD} — {len(heatmap_df):,} of {len(HEATMAP_DF):,} "
      f"simulated locations ({len(heatmap_df) / len(HEATMAP_DF):.0%}) from "
      f"{N_HEATMAP_TRAJ} trajectories")
print(f"Heatmap grid: {heatmap.shape[0]} x {heatmap.shape[1]} cells of "
      f"{PIXEL_SIZE * HEATMAP_AGG:.0f} m")
print(f"{heatmap.sum():,} locations counted after dropping the first {BURN_IN} steps "
      f"of each trajectory")
print(f"{(heatmap > 0).sum():,} occupied cells, up to {heatmap.max():,} locations in one cell")


Period: full — 46,300,000 of 46,300,000 simulated locations (100%) from 2500 trajectories
Heatmap grid: 668 x 858 cells of 40 m
43,800,000 locations counted after dropping the first 1000 steps of each trajectory
499,952 occupied cells, up to 51,340 locations in one cell

Counts are drawn on a log colour scale — a handful of cells in some cells usually hold an order of magnitude more locations than the rest (possibly due to bias towards the release sites or getting ‘stuck’ in certain areas), which would flatten a linear scale to a single bright dot. Empty cells are masked so the landscape shows through.

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
Betweenness
Quantifies the importance of different elements of the matrix in facilitating connectivity between other patches or habitats within the landscape. It identifies key corridors or bottlenecks that serve as critical links for maintaining overall connectivity in the landscape. It is calculated as the number of times the simulated individuals enter each raster cell (which are typically aggregated to a coarser scale than the spatial covariates used in the simulations). Betweenness measures the importance of each cell within the landscape for maintaining functional connectivity
Adapted from: https://github.com/DavidDHofmann/DispersalSimulation/blob/main/AWDCaseStudy/02_Analysis/09_Betweenness.R

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
How it is calculated here
Following the R script, in four steps:

A coarse grid of nodes. The landscape rasters are 20 m, much finer than the scale connectivity is meaningful at, so they are aggregated by BETWEENNESS_AGG into 500 m cells. Each cell is one node in the network. The grid keeps the rasters’ origin and CRS, so it lines up with the covariates and with the heatmap above.
Transitions become edges. Every simulated path is walked cell by cell, and each move from one cell into the next is an edge. A trajectory contributes a given (from, to) pair once, however often it repeats it (singlecount = TRUE in the R script), so the pooled count is “how many of the simulated pigs ever made this move”, not “how many times it happened”.
Edge weights invert the counts: weight = mean(count) / count. networkx reads the weight as a cost, so a transition many pigs made is cheap and shortest paths follow the routes the simulation actually took.
Betweenness of a node is the number of those shortest paths running through it. Cells with high betweenness are the ones movement is funnelled through.


path_cells() and transition_counts()

Inputs

BETWEENNESS_DF

simulated locations, as returned by simulate_trajectories() — the same input trajectory_heatmap() takes.

BETWEENNESS_AGG

aggregate agg x agg raster pixels into one network cell. Betweenness is an all-pairs shortest path calculation, so the node count sets the runtime: 500 m cells give 3,672 nodes and about a minute, 250 m cells give 15,651 and about twenty.

BETWEENNESS_EPS

spacing, in cell widths, at which each step is densified before the cells under it are read off. Simulated steps have a median length of ~26 m but reach ~700 m, so a long step can jump clean over a 500 m cell; densifying catches it.

BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN, BETWEENNESS_MAX_STEPS

drop the first n steps of every trajectory, then keep at most m of what is left.

BETWEENNESS_K

None computes betweenness exactly; an integer estimates it from that many randomly chosen pivot nodes, which is what makes a finer grid tractable.


Outputs: betweenness — a float32 array on the coarsened grid, plus its affine transform bet_transform, ready for save_raster() and add_heatmap_overlay() just like the heatmap.

Betweenness is not the heatmap. The heatmap counts where the pigs were; betweenness counts the routes needed to get between places. A large open area can hold many locations and little betweenness, while a narrow crossing holds few locations and a lot of it. On the 1,000-step run the two surfaces correlate at only rho ~ 0.55 across the cells they share — related, but far from the same map. If they ever come out looking identical, something is wrong.
BETWEENNESS_MAX_STEPS matters more than it looks. Given enough steps every trajectory eventually visits most of the landscape, every adjacent pair of cells picks up an edge from nearly every trajectory, the weights flatten towards uniform, and betweenness ends up describing the grid rather than the movement. On the 599-trajectory run, the network covers 1,658 of the 3,672 cells after 1,000 steps, 3,348 after 10,000, and 3,671 — all but one — after 100,000. The R script handles this by recomputing the map at several step budgets (design$steps = c(125, 500, 2000)) and checking the pattern has settled; the same is worth doing here.

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
Wet season


Show code
BETWEENNESS_DF        = sim_many  # trajectories to build the network from
BETWEENNESS_AGG       = 5              # network cell = AGG x AGG raster pixels (n x 20 m)
BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN   = 1000              # drop the first n steps of every trajectory
BETWEENNESS_MAX_STEPS = 2500         # ...and keep at most this many of what is left
BETWEENNESS_PERIOD    = "wet"         # "full", "wet" or "dry" — as for the heatmap
BETWEENNESS_EPS       = 0.25           # densify each step to this spacing, in cell widths
BETWEENNESS_K         = 1000           # None = exact; an int samples that many pivot nodes
BETWEENNESS_EDGE      = 2              # blank this many network cells around the border (x BET_CELL_M m) - this is at the aggregated network cell level, not the original raster pixel level


# The network grid: the landscape rasters' origin and CRS with cells AGG times larger.
# ceil() rather than round() so the grid covers the whole raster — the same arithmetic
# trajectory_heatmap() uses, which is what makes the two grids line up cell for cell.
bet_height = math.ceil(landscape_tensors[0].shape[0] / BETWEENNESS_AGG)
bet_width  = math.ceil(landscape_tensors[0].shape[1] / BETWEENNESS_AGG)
bet_transform = raster_transform * Affine.scale(BETWEENNESS_AGG)
N_NODES = bet_height * bet_width
BET_CELL_M = PIXEL_SIZE * BETWEENNESS_AGG


def path_cells(x, y, eps=BETWEENNESS_EPS):
    """The sequence of network cells one simulated path passes through.

    Points outside the raster come back as -1 rather than being dropped, so that
    a pig which leaves the landscape and returns does not look like one long
    move between the cells either side of the excursion.
    """
    col, row = ~bet_transform * (np.asarray(x, dtype=float), np.asarray(y, dtype=float))
    if col.size < 2:
        return np.empty(0, dtype=np.int64)

    # Densify each step into enough sub-points that none can skip over a cell.
    # Most steps are far shorter than a cell and get n_sub = 1, so this costs
    # little; the occasional ~700 m step is the reason it is here at all.
    dcol, drow = np.diff(col), np.diff(row)
    n_sub = np.maximum(1, np.ceil(np.hypot(dcol, drow) / eps)).astype(np.int64)
    seg   = np.repeat(np.arange(n_sub.size), n_sub)      # step each sub-point belongs to
    start = np.repeat(np.cumsum(n_sub) - n_sub, n_sub)   # index of that step's first one
    frac  = (np.arange(n_sub.sum()) - start) / np.repeat(n_sub, n_sub)
    # Each step contributes its start and the points along it; the very last
    # location is the start of no step, so it is appended by hand.
    col_i = np.append(col[seg] + frac * dcol[seg], col[-1])
    row_i = np.append(row[seg] + frac * drow[seg], row[-1])

    c = np.floor(col_i).astype(np.int64)
    r = np.floor(row_i).astype(np.int64)
    inside = (r >= 0) & (r < bet_height) & (c >= 0) & (c < bet_width)
    node = np.where(inside, r * bet_width + c, -1)   # node ids run in raster order
    # Consecutive sub-points usually land in the same cell.  Keeping only the
    # changes leaves one entry per cell entered, and no from == to self-loops.
    return node[np.r_[True, node[1:] != node[:-1]]]


def transition_counts(df, id_col="trajectory_id"):
    """Pool cell-to-cell transitions over every trajectory.

    A trajectory contributes each (from, to) pair once however often it repeats
    it, so the counts returned are the number of *trajectories* that ever made
    each move.  Trajectories are handled one at a time rather than as a single
    array: at 599 x 100,000 locations the intermediate keys would otherwise run
    to several GB.
    """
    keys, n_edge_drops = [], 0
    for _tid, sub in df.groupby(id_col, sort=True):
        node = path_cells(sub["x"].to_numpy(), sub["y"].to_numpy())
        if node.size < 2:
            continue
        src, dst = node[:-1], node[1:]
        ok = (src >= 0) & (dst >= 0)          # drop moves touching the outside
        n_edge_drops += int((~ok).sum())
        keys.append(np.unique(src[ok] * N_NODES + dst[ok]))
    if not keys:
        raise ValueError(
            "no transitions — no trajectory entered more than one network cell"
        )
    key, count = np.unique(np.concatenate(keys), return_counts=True)
    return key // N_NODES, key % N_NODES, count, n_edge_drops


print(f"Network grid: {bet_height} x {bet_width} = {N_NODES:,} cells of {BET_CELL_M:.0f} m")


Network grid: 267 x 343 = 91,581 cells of 100 m



Build the network and calculate betweenness
The period filter is the same filter_period() the heatmap uses, so a betweenness surface and a heatmap built with the same PERIOD describe the same slice of the year.


Show code
bet_df = filter_period(BETWEENNESS_DF, BETWEENNESS_PERIOD)

# renumber steps sequentially within the period (closes the gaps between seasons)
bet_df["step_seq"] = bet_df.groupby("trajectory_id")["step"].rank(method="dense").astype(int) - 1

# drop the first n steps of every trajectory, and keep at most the next m steps.
bet_df = bet_df[
    (bet_df["step_seq"] >= BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN)
    & (bet_df["step_seq"] < BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN + BETWEENNESS_MAX_STEPS)
]

# check that there are simulated locations for this period
if bet_df.empty:
    raise ValueError(
        f"no simulated locations left — steps {BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN} to "
        f"{BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN + BETWEENNESS_MAX_STEPS} of the "
        f"{BETWEENNESS_PERIOD} season is outside what was simulated"
    )

# Reused by the plot, GeoTIFF and web map below so they all describe the same subset.
N_BET_TRAJ = bet_df["trajectory_id"].nunique()
BET_TAG = f"_{BETWEENNESS_PERIOD}"

t0 = time.time()
bet_src, bet_dst, bet_count, n_edge_drops = transition_counts(bet_df)
print(f"Period: {BETWEENNESS_PERIOD} — {len(bet_df):,} locations from {N_BET_TRAJ} "
      f"trajectories, steps {BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN} to "
      f"{BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN + BETWEENNESS_MAX_STEPS - 1}")
print(f"{len(bet_src):,} unique transitions found in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s "
      f"({n_edge_drops:,} dropped at the raster edge)")

# networkx reads the weight as a cost, so invert the counts: a transition many
# trajectories made is cheap, and shortest paths prefer it.
bet_weight = bet_count.mean() / bet_count

# Every cell is a node, including the ones no trajectory reached — they sit in the
# network isolated and score zero, as `vertices = ver` does in the R script.
bet_net = nx.DiGraph()
bet_net.add_nodes_from(range(N_NODES))
bet_net.add_weighted_edges_from(
    zip(bet_src.tolist(), bet_dst.tolist(), bet_weight.tolist(), strict=True)
)
print(f"Network: {bet_net.number_of_nodes():,} nodes, {bet_net.number_of_edges():,} edges")

t0 = time.time()
bet_scores = nx.betweenness_centrality(
    bet_net, k=BETWEENNESS_K, weight="weight", normalized=False, seed=1
)
print(f"Betweenness computed in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s"
      + ("" if BETWEENNESS_K is None else f" (approximate, {BETWEENNESS_K} pivots)"))

# Cells no trajectory ever entered are left as NaN rather than 0, so the map can
# tell them apart from cells that are in the network but on no shortest path.
in_network = np.zeros(N_NODES, dtype=bool)
in_network[bet_src] = True
in_network[bet_dst] = True
betweenness = np.full(N_NODES, np.nan, dtype=np.float32)
betweenness[in_network] = [bet_scores[n] for n in np.flatnonzero(in_network)]
betweenness = betweenness.reshape(bet_height, bet_width)

# Blank a border of cells to remove edge effects.  The network is still built on
# the full grid, so paths that pass near the edge still count towards interior
# cells; only the edge scores themselves are discarded.  The shape is unchanged,
# so the raster still stacks with the others on bet_transform.
if BETWEENNESS_EDGE > 0:
    e = BETWEENNESS_EDGE

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
Dry season


Show code
BETWEENNESS_PERIOD    = "dry"         # "full", "wet" or "dry" — as for the heatmap



Build the network and calculate betweenness
The period filter is the same filter_period() the heatmap uses, so a betweenness surface and a heatmap built with the same PERIOD describe the same slice of the year.


Show code
bet_df = filter_period(BETWEENNESS_DF, BETWEENNESS_PERIOD)

# renumber steps sequentially within the period (closes the gaps between seasons)
bet_df["step_seq"] = bet_df.groupby("trajectory_id")["step"].rank(method="dense").astype(int) - 1

# drop the first n steps of every trajectory, and keep at most the next m steps.
bet_df = bet_df[
    (bet_df["step_seq"] >= BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN)
    & (bet_df["step_seq"] < BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN + BETWEENNESS_MAX_STEPS)
]

# check that there are simulated locations for this period
if bet_df.empty:
    raise ValueError(
        f"no simulated locations left — steps {BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN} to "
        f"{BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN + BETWEENNESS_MAX_STEPS} of the "
        f"{BETWEENNESS_PERIOD} season is outside what was simulated"
    )

# Reused by the plot, GeoTIFF and web map below so they all describe the same subset.
N_BET_TRAJ = bet_df["trajectory_id"].nunique()
BET_TAG = f"_{BETWEENNESS_PERIOD}"

t0 = time.time()
bet_src, bet_dst, bet_count, n_edge_drops = transition_counts(bet_df)
print(f"Period: {BETWEENNESS_PERIOD} — {len(bet_df):,} locations from {N_BET_TRAJ} "
      f"trajectories, steps {BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN} to "
      f"{BETWEENNESS_BURN_IN + BETWEENNESS_MAX_STEPS - 1}")
print(f"{len(bet_src):,} unique transitions found in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s "
      f"({n_edge_drops:,} dropped at the raster edge)")

# networkx reads the weight as a cost, so invert the counts: a transition many
# trajectories made is cheap, and shortest paths prefer it.
bet_weight = bet_count.mean() / bet_count

# Every cell is a node, including the ones no trajectory reached — they sit in the
# network isolated and score zero, as `vertices = ver` does in the R script.
bet_net = nx.DiGraph()
bet_net.add_nodes_from(range(N_NODES))
bet_net.add_weighted_edges_from(
    zip(bet_src.tolist(), bet_dst.tolist(), bet_weight.tolist(), strict=True)
)
print(f"Network: {bet_net.number_of_nodes():,} nodes, {bet_net.number_of_edges():,} edges")

t0 = time.time()
bet_scores = nx.betweenness_centrality(
    bet_net, k=BETWEENNESS_K, weight="weight", normalized=False, seed=1
)
print(f"Betweenness computed in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s"
      + ("" if BETWEENNESS_K is None else f" (approximate, {BETWEENNESS_K} pivots)"))

# Cells no trajectory ever entered are left as NaN rather than 0, so the map can
# tell them apart from cells that are in the network but on no shortest path.
in_network = np.zeros(N_NODES, dtype=bool)
in_network[bet_src] = True
in_network[bet_dst] = True
betweenness = np.full(N_NODES, np.nan, dtype=np.float32)
betweenness[in_network] = [bet_scores[n] for n in np.flatnonzero(in_network)]
betweenness = betweenness.reshape(bet_height, bet_width)

# Blank a border of cells to remove edge effects.  The network is still built on
# the full grid, so paths that pass near the edge still count towards interior
# cells; only the edge scores themselves are discarded.  The shape is unchanged,
# so the raster still stacks with the others on bet_transform.
if BETWEENNESS_EDGE > 0:
    e = BETWEENNESS_EDGE
    betweenness[:e, :]  = np.nan
    betweenness[-e:, :] = np.nan
    betweenness[:, :e]  = np.nan
    betweenness[:, -e:] = np.nan

print(f"{in_network.sum():,} of {N_NODES:,} cells were entered by at least one "
      f"trajectory; betweenness runs from 0 to {np.nanmax(betweenness):,.0f}")

# simplified names for the BOM weather variables (new name = original BOM name), used for both stations
weather_names <- c(

  air_temp_c = "Air Temperature in degrees C",

  rel_humidity_pct = "Relative humidity in percentage %",
  wind_speed_kmh = "Wind speed in km/h",

  cloud_height_2_ft = "Ceilometer cloud height (of second group) in feet",

  cloud_height_3_ft = "Ceilometer cloud height (of third group) in feet",
  sky_clear_flag = "Ceilometer sky clear flag"
)

# the original names are used as plot labels, plus a label for the derived half-hourly rain
weather_labels <- c(weather_names,
                    rain_30min_mm = "Precipitation in the previous 30 minutes in mm")
weather_labels[] <- stringr::str_squish(weather_labels) # removes the double space in the gust name

# save the labels for the analysis scripts
write_csv(tibble::enframe(weather_labels, name = "variable", value = "label"),
          "data/weather_variable_labels.csv")

oenpelli_weather <- oenpelli_weather_full %>%
  dplyr::select(-hm, -`Station Number`, -matches("quality", ignore.case = TRUE),
                -matches("Ceilometer"), -`AWS Flag`, -`#`) %>%
  # combine the date/time components, which are in local standard time (Darwin has no daylight saving)
  dplyr::mutate(
    datetime = lubridate::make_datetime(
      year = `Year Month Day Hour Minutes in YYYY`,
      month = as.integer(MM),
      day = as.integer(DD),
      hour = as.integer(HH24),
      min = as.integer(`MI format in Local standard time`),
      tz = "Australia/Darwin"),
    .before = 1) %>%
  dplyr::select(-`Year Month Day Hour Minutes in YYYY`, -MM, -DD, -HH24,
                -`MI format in Local standard time`) %>%
  # any_of() as the cloud columns aren't recorded at Oenpelli
  dplyr::rename(dplyr::any_of(weather_names)) %>%
  # rain in each half-hour - the since-9am total resets after the 9:00 reading, so group by
  # rain day (9:30 to 9:00 the next day) and subtract the previous reading
  dplyr::mutate(rain_day = lubridate::as_date(datetime - lubridate::minutes(570))) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(rain_day) %>%
  # round to remove floating point error from the subtraction (gauge resolution is 0.2 mm)
  dplyr::mutate(rain_30min_mm = round(rain_since_9am_mm - dplyr::lag(rain_since_9am_mm, default = 0), 1),
                .after = rain_since_9am_mm) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::select(-rain_day) %>%
  dplyr::rename_with(~ paste0("onpli_", .x))

              all.x = TRUE, sort = FALSE)

title: Shooting responses
section: Distance in time and space of pig GPS locations to shooting events
text:
Distance in time and space of pig GPS locations to shooting events


Show code
# find all pig/shooting pairs within x m (returns a list of indices)
# this is irrespective of time at this point
idx <- st_is_within_distance(pig_all_steps_sf, filtered_shooting_locations, dist = 500)

# turn that into a table of matched pairs
# this means that this pig GPS location is within x m of this shooting location
pairs <- tibble(
  pig_row   = rep(seq_along(idx), lengths(idx)),
  shoot_row = unlist(idx)
)

# distance between pig GPS points and shooting locations in metres
pairs$dist_m <- as.numeric(
  st_distance(pig_all_steps_sf[pairs$pig_row, ],
              filtered_shooting_locations[pairs$shoot_row, ],
              by_element = TRUE)
)

# attach the attributes from both objects
hits <- bind_cols(
  # keep only the GPS locations that are within x m of a shooting location
  pig_all_steps_sf[pairs$pig_row, ],
  filtered_shooting_locations[pairs$shoot_row, ] %>% st_drop_geometry(), #%>% rename_with(~ paste0("shoot_", .x)),
  dist_m = pairs$dist_m
)

# keep only the GPS locations that are within 3 hours of a shooting event
# also add the time difference between the pig GPS location and the shooting event (in hours)
# negative values are before the shooting event, positive values are after 
hits <- hits %>% 
  filter(t1_ >= shoot_time - hours(3),
         t1_ <= shoot_time + hours(3)) %>% 
  mutate(
    shoot_time_diff = as.numeric(difftime(t1_, shoot_time, units = "hours")),
  ) 



Keep only the nearest in time
For each shooting location and each pig, take the pig GPS location that is nearest in time to the shooting event.
For instance, within 3 hours either side of the shooting times, we have 182 instances where a pig was within 2000 m of a shooting event. What we have left in this dataframe is the ‘focal shooting location’, meaning it was nearest in time to the shooting event for that pig.
Using the focal shooting location, we will extract a sequence of locations from before and after the shooting event, to see if there is a change in behaviour.


Show code
hits_nearest_time <- hits %>% 
  group_by(name, shoot_id) %>% 
  slice_min(abs(shoot_time_diff), n = 1)  %>% 
  ungroup()

hits_nearest_time



  



Show code
# there are four periods with a couple days of shooting
ggplot(hits_nearest_time, aes(x = shoot_time)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "red", colour = "black") +
  scale_x_datetime("Time difference between pig GPS location and shooting event (hours)") +
  theme_bw()











Extract pig GPS locations either side of the focal shoot location


Show code
shoot_focal_window <- 24 # time either side of focal shooting location (in hours)

# one row per pig/shooting instance, with the temporal window to filter the data by
focal <- hits_nearest_time %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  distinct(name, shoot_id, shoot_time) %>%
  mutate(win_start = shoot_time - hours(shoot_focal_window),
         win_end   = shoot_time + hours(shoot_focal_window))

# shooting locations, one row per shoot_id
shoot_geom <- filtered_shooting_locations %>%
  select(shoot_id)

# distance (m) from each fix to the pig's own GPS fix nearest in time to the shoot
# (i.e. where the pig was at t = 0), so every sequence starts from 0 at the shoot.
# Staying near 0 after the shoot suggests bunkering down, rapid increases suggest fleeing
add_dist_to_t0 <- function(seqs) {
  seqs %>%
    group_by(seq_id) %>%
    mutate(
      dist_to_t0_m = as.numeric(
        st_distance(geometry, geometry[which.min(abs(time_diff_hrs))]))
    ) %>%
    ungroup()
}

# pull every GPS fix for that pig inside the window
shooting_sequences <- pig_all_steps_sf %>%
  inner_join(focal,
             by = join_by(name, between(t1_, win_start, win_end)),
             relationship = "many-to-many")

# distance (m) from each fix to its own focal shooting location
shooting_sequences <- shooting_sequences %>%
  mutate(
    dist_to_shoot_m = as.numeric(
      st_distance(geometry,
                  shoot_geom$geometry[match(shoot_id, shoot_geom$shoot_id)],
                  by_element = TRUE)),
    time_diff_hrs = as.numeric(difftime(t1_, shoot_time, units = "hours")),
    period = if_else(time_diff_hrs < 0, "baseline", "response"),
    seq_id = paste(name, shoot_id, sep = "_")
  ) %>%
  arrange(seq_id, t1_) %>%
  add_dist_to_t0()

head(shooting_sequences, 10) # printing every row bloats the rendered html



  





Just use the first matching shoot of each day
Often, there are multiple shooting locations on the same day - we will therefore only look at the first shooting event for each pig on that day, and the GPS locations either side of that event.


Show code
shooting_sequences_daily <- shooting_sequences %>% 
  mutate(
    shoot_date = lubridate::as_date(shoot_time)
  ) %>% 
  group_by(name, shoot_date) %>% 
  slice_min(shoot_time, n = 1)  %>% 
  ungroup()

head(shooting_sequences_daily, 10)

title: Shooting responses
text:
Distance to the shooting location
Here we are looking at the distance of the pig GPS locations to the shooting location, relative to the time of the shooting event. The red dashed line is the time of the shooting event. title: Shooting responses
text:
5 days before each shooting operation
Given the fairly consistent time of shooting operations (in the morning), we don’t know whether the behavioural patterns that we are observing are due to the shooting or just their typical behaviour for those times of day.
For this, we will generate a control for comparison. Given that each of the shooting events covered a couple days, we will take sequences of locations from the pigs that were exposed to shooting, at the same time of day as each of the shooting events, but 5 days before the actual shooting events.
We run essentially the same code, but just subtract 5 days from the sequences that we use to extract locations.


Show code
pseudo_interval <- lubridate::days(5)

# One row per focal pig/shooting event, with the temporal window
focal_pseudo <- hits_nearest_time %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  distinct(name, shoot_id, shoot_time) %>%
  mutate(
    shoot_time = shoot_time - pseudo_interval,
    win_start = shoot_time - hours(shoot_focal_window),
    win_end   = shoot_time + hours(shoot_focal_window)
    )

# Shooting locations, same CRS as the pigs, one row per shoot_id
shoot_geom <- filtered_shooting_locations %>%
  select(shoot_id)

# Pull every GPS fix for that pig inside the window
seqs_pseudo <- pig_all_steps_sf %>% 
  inner_join(focal_pseudo,
             by = join_by(name, between(t1_, win_start, win_end)),
             relationship = "many-to-many")

# Distance (m) from each fix to its own focal shooting location
seqs_pseudo <- seqs_pseudo %>%
  mutate(
    dist_to_shoot_m = as.numeric(
      st_distance(geometry,
                  shoot_geom$geometry[match(shoot_id, shoot_geom$shoot_id)],
                  by_element = TRUE)),
    time_diff_hrs = as.numeric(difftime(t1_, shoot_time, units = "hours")),
    period = if_else(time_diff_hrs < 0, "baseline", "response"),
    seq_id = paste(name, shoot_id, sep = "_")
  ) %>%
  arrange(seq_id, t1_) %>%
  add_dist_to_t0()

text:
Same time but far away
Here we get locations for pigs that have locations at the same time as the shooting events, but which were more than 5 km away.


Show code
shoot_distance <- 10000  # metres

# add an ID to the shooting locations
shoot <- filtered_shooting_locations %>%
  mutate(shoot_id = row_number())

# add an ID to the pig GPS locations
pig <- pig_all_steps_sf %>%
  mutate(pig_row = row_number())

# initial matching window - just grab the pig locations that are 
# within three hours of the shooting locations
window <- 3 * 3600  # seconds; narrow this if you want "same time" more strictly

# time-match pairs 
pairs <- pig %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(name, pig_row, t1_) %>%                        # your pig timestamp column
  inner_join(
    shoot %>%
      st_drop_geometry() %>%
      transmute(shoot_id, shoot_time,          # your shooting timestamp column
                lo = shoot_time - window,
                hi = shoot_time + window),
    by = join_by(between(t1_, lo, hi))
  )

# distance for each matched pair only
pairs$dist_m <- st_distance(
  st_geometry(pig)[pairs$pig_row],
  st_geometry(shoot)[pairs$shoot_id],
  by_element = TRUE
) %>% as.numeric()

hist(pairs$dist_m)









Show code

  filter(dist_m > shoot_distance) %>% 
  mutate(

Set up the paired data


Show code
# time windows (hours relative to the shoot) for the paired comparisons
# windows include their start and exclude their end, so the fix at t = 0 is in the first window after the shoot
paired_breaks <- c(-3, 0, 3, 6, 12, 24)
paired_labels <- c("3-0 h before", "0-3 h after", "3-6 h after", "6-12 h after", "12-24 h after")

paired_data <- shooting_sequences_daily_all %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(type %in% c("Observed", "Pseudo")) %>%
  mutate(window = cut(time_diff_hrs, breaks = paired_breaks, labels = paired_labels, right = FALSE)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(window))

# number of sequences that have both an observed and a control sequence
paired_data %>%
  distinct(type, seq_id) %>%
  count(type)



  



Show code
# Wilcoxon signed-rank test of whether the paired differences are centred on 0,
# with Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values across all the tests in the table
paired_wilcox <- function(diffs, ...) {
  diffs %>%
    group_by(...) %>%
    summarise(
      n           = sum(!is.na(diff)),
      median_diff = median(diff, na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_diff   = mean(diff, na.rm = TRUE),
      # returns NA when all differences are 0 (e.g. a vegetation class that was never used)
      p_value     = if (all(diff == 0, na.rm = TRUE)) NA_real_ else
                      suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(diff, mu = 0, exact = FALSE)$p.value),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"))
}

# histogram of the paired differences, with 0 (dashed) and the median difference (solid)
plot_paired_diffs <- function(diffs, tests, x_lab, title, digits = 2) {

  tests <- tests %>%
    mutate(label = paste0("n = ", n,
                          "\nmean = ", round(mean_diff, digits),
                          "\np = ", signif(p_value, 2),
                          "\np adj = ", signif(p_adj, 2)))

  diffs %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = diff)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = shoot_cols["Observed"], colour = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_rug(colour = shoot_cols["Observed"], alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_vline(data = tests, aes(xintercept = mean_diff), colour = shoot_cols["Observed"], linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_text(data = tests, aes(x = Inf, y = Inf, label = label),
              hjust = 1.05, vjust = 1.1, size = 2.5, lineheight = 0.9) +
    scale_y_continuous("Number of pairs", expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.6))) +
    labs(x = x_lab, title = title,
         subtitle = "Observed shoot minus the same pig 5 days before") +
    theme_bw()
}

text:
Vegetation classes
Proportion of fixes in each vegetation class within each window. Positive differences mean the pig used that class more on the shoot day than 5 days before. Classes that a pig never used in either sequence contribute a difference of 0, so classes that are rarely used will have most of their differences at exactly 0.

# Reproducibility — fix random seeds so results are the same on every run.

# train/val/test partition changes every run and two training configurations
# cannot be compared.

# DEVICE is capitalised — module-level constant (set once, never reassigned).
# get_device() returns 'cuda' if a GPU is available, 'mps' on Apple Silicon,
# or 'cpu' otherwise.  All tensors and the model are moved to this device.

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
Set script paths
If you have cloned/forked/downloaded the GitHub repo (https://github.com/swforrest/deepSSF_package) you shouldn’t need to change these, but for your own analyses you will want to set these to point to where your data is and where you want outputs saved.
All-caps names below are module-level constants — set once here and referenced throughout the notebook without being reassigned. Python has no built-in constant keyword, so capitalisation is the community convention (PEP 8) to signal “do not change this value”.


Show code
DATA_DIR = Path("data")  # location of the bundled sample data
MAPPING_DIR = Path("mapping")  # location of the landcover mapping files
CSV_PATH = DATA_DIR / "pigs_east_alligator_steps_covs_20261015.csv"  # GPS tracking data

# NOTE: 's2' and 's2_dir' are RESERVED keys in load_environmental_layers().
# 's2_dir' triggers the monthly-composite loader (load_s2_data), and a plain
# 's2' entry is skipped by the per-file loop — so a single multi-band GeoTIFF
# must be given any *other* name, otherwise nothing is loaded and the function
# raises "raster_transform could not be set".
LAYER_PATHS = {
    # Topographic layers (DEM, slope)
    "dem": str(MAPPING_DIR / "DEM_east_alligator_3112.tif"),
    "slope": str(MAPPING_DIR / "slope_east_alligator_3112.tif"),
    "water": str(MAPPING_DIR / "water_layer_east_alligator.tif"),

    # 3-band Sentinel-2 composite: NDVI, NDWI, NDMI (20 m, EPSG:3112)
    # "s2_indices": str(MAPPING_DIR / "feral_pig_aoi_S2_indices_2025-09-12_to_2026-06-23.tif"),

    # Alternative — all 12 S2 bands (12 spatial channels instead of 3, slower to train):
    # "s2_median": str(MAPPING_DIR / "feral_pig_aoi_S2_median_full_2025-09-12_to_2026-06-23.tif"),

    # AlphaEarth embeddings (2025)
    "alphaearth": str(MAPPING_DIR / "alphaearth_2025_east_alligator_3112.tif"),
}
                 
OUTPUT_DIR = deepssf.get_output_dir(base="outputs/alphaearth")   # figures and model checkpoints go here - function adds date and index
# OUTPUT_DIR = Path("outputs/alphaearth/2026-10-29_1")  # manually set to match the training run used to generate the model

print(f"Output directory: {OUTPUT_DIR}")
SNAPSHOT_DIR = OUTPUT_DIR / "training_snapshots"  # per-batch prediction-map snapshots

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
load_environmental_layers()
Reads each GeoTIFF listed in LAYER_PATHS, min–max

Scales every band to [0, 1], and returns:

env_layers — dict mapping layer name → NumPy array: 2-D (H × W) for single-band GeoTIFFs, 3-D (bands × H × W) for multi-band ones, where each band becomes its own model input channel
raster_transform — Affine object that converts pixel (row, col) indices to the projected coordinates (easting, northing) of the raster(s), which should be in the same CRS as the GPS data. This transform is used whenever we need to translate between pixel space and real-world coordinates.


Two things to watch for:

The keys 's2' and 's2_dir' are reserved for the monthly Sentinel-2 composite loader — a single GeoTIFF passed under the name 's2' is silently skipped (see the note in the paths cell above).
The rescaling uses a single global min/max across all bands of a file, and computes (data - lo) / hi rather than (data - lo) / (hi - lo). Our index raster is int16 scaled by 10 000 with ±10 000 fill values, so the loaded values span [0, 2] rather than [0, 1] and the three indices are not individually normalised. That is workable (the CNN can rescale internally) but if it hurts training, pre-scale each band yourself and save as .npy — non-.tif paths in LAYER_PATHS are loaded with np.load(..., mmap_mode='r') and left untouched, though at least one real .tif must remain in the dict so the transform can be set.



Show code
env_layers, raster_transform = deepssf.load_environmental_layers(LAYER_PATHS)
print("Layers loaded:", list(env_layers.keys()))
for name, arr in env_layers.items():
    print(f"  {name}: shape={arr.shape}, min={arr.min():.3f}, max={arr.max():.3f}")

# Each band of a multi-band layer becomes one CNN input channel, so count bands
# (not layers) here and reuse the total when setting ModelParams below.  Deriving
# it means switching rasters in LAYER_PATHS needs no other edits.
N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS = sum(1 if arr.ndim == 2 else arr.shape[0] for arr in env_layers.values())
print(f"Spatial channels: {N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS}")

This confirms the raster extent covers the animal’s home range and gives a visual sense of the landscape the model will learn from.

# Flatten env_layers into one (2-D array, label) pair per spatial channel so the
# figure adapts to whatever LAYER_PATHS provides (1 layer of 3 bands, 2 layers of
# 1 band, ...).  Band descriptions come from the GeoTIFF metadata where present.
plot_n_layers = 9  # limit the number of layers plotted to avoid a huge figure

for name, arr in env_layers.items():

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
prepare_movement_df()
Converts a fixes dataframe (one row per GPS location) into a step dataframe (one row per movement between consecutive fixes).

For each step it computes:

dx, dy — displacement in projected CRS units (metres)
bearing — direction of travel (radians; 0 = north, clockwise positive)
bearing_tm1 — bearing of the previous step, used as a model input so the network can capture directional persistence by estimating a turning angle
dt_hour — time elapsed between consecutive fixes (hours)
hour_t1, yday_t1 — decimal hour-of-day and day-of-year at the step start location
*_sin1 / *_cos1 — sine/cosine encodings of hour and yday (see SCALAR_COLS below)


The “1” on column names (x1_, y1_, t1_, etc.) flags them as “start of step” variables; and the “2” in x2_, y2_, t2_ are the corresponding “end of step” values, following the convention of the amt package (Signer et al. 2019). The last fix for each individual is dropped because no forward step can be formed.


Show code
# The CSV is already in amt step format, but prepare_movement_df() expects one row
# per *fix* and rebuilds the steps itself (it also derives bearing, dt_hour and the
# cyclic time encodings the model needs).  Point it at the step-start columns and
# let it re-form the steps from consecutive fixes.
step_df = deepssf.prepare_movement_df(
    raw_df, 
    id_col="name", 
    time_col="t1_", 
    x_col="x1_", 
    y_col="y1_"
)
n_dropped = len(raw_df) - len(step_df)
print(f"Movement steps : {len(step_df):,}  ({n_dropped} dropped — last per individual)")

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
SCALAR_COLS
These are non-spatial inputs. For processing with convolutional layers, they are converted into spatial windows (rasters/arrays), and stacked with the truly spatial covariates.
The model receives a fixed-size spatial window centred on each step’s start location. To let the network express time-varying habitat preferences (e.g. different nocturnal vs diurnal use), scalar covariates are tiled into additional channels of the same H × W size, so every pixel “knows” the current time context when habitat suitability is estimated.

hour_t1_sin1 / hour_t1_cos1

Sine and cosine of (2π × hour / 24), encoding time-of-day as a circular variable. The circular encoding means 23:00 and 01:00 are treated as adjacent — a plain hour value would have an artificial discontinuity at midnight.

yday_t1_sin1 / yday_t1_cos1

Same circular encoding for day-of-year (1–365), capturing seasonal variation in habitat use (e.g. dry-season vs wet-season movements).

dt_hour

Elapsed time between consecutive fixes (hours). Because GPS collars do not always fix at a perfectly regular rate, including dt_hour lets the movement kernel rescale expected displacement proportionally to the actual time interval rather than assuming a fixed fix rate. Note: dt_hour must be supplied at simulation time as well, so that simulate_trajectory() produces inputs consistent with training.




Show code
SCALAR_COLS = ["hour_t1_sin1",
               "hour_t1_cos1", 
               "yday_t1_sin1", 
               "yday_t1_cos1", 
               "dt_hour"]

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
PIXEL_SIZE
Raster resolution in CRS units (metres here). Read straight off raster_transform rather than typed in: the transform is the authority on the grid the model is trained against, and a hand-entered value that disagrees with it silently mis-scales the movement kernel — which is parameterised in metres — against a grid measured in pixels.


Show code
# transform.a is the cell width, transform.e the (negative) cell height
PIXEL_SIZE = abs(raster_transform.a)

if not math.isclose(abs(raster_transform.a), abs(raster_transform.e)):
    raise ValueError(
        f"Non-square pixels ({abs(raster_transform.a)} x {abs(raster_transform.e)}); "
        "the model assumes square cells."
    )

print(f"Pixel size: {PIXEL_SIZE} m")


Pixel size: 20.0 m

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
WINDOW_SIZE
The size of the local availability window in cells/pixels.
The maximum step length that the model will allow is the distance between the centre cell and the nearest edge (in reality some steps may be longer if they are in the corners).


Show code
WINDOW_SIZE = 51

print(f"Pixel size: {PIXEL_SIZE} m  →  window {WINDOW_SIZE} px = "
      f"{WINDOW_SIZE * PIXEL_SIZE:,.0f} m across")

print(f"Maximum possible step: {((WINDOW_SIZE - 1) / 2) * PIXEL_SIZE:,.0f} m")


Pixel size: 20.0 m  →  window 51 px = 1,020 m across
Maximum possible step: 500 m

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
BATCH_SIZE
Number of training samples (movement steps) per training mini-batch


Show code
BATCH_SIZE  = 128

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE
How many convolutional layers in the movement subnetwork of the model?
Each of the convolution layers has a max pooling layer, so more layers will result in greater dimension reduction that will feed into the fully-connected layer that outputs the movement parameters.


Show code
N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE = 4

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
N_CONV_LAYERS_HAB
How many convolutional layers in the habitat selection subnetwork of the model?
These convolution layers do not have max pooling layers, so there is no dimension reduction. More layers will increase the depth of the model and allow for more abstracted features to be identified, but will slow model training/prediction.
This count includes the final convolution layer, which is the one that collapses the feature maps down to the single-channel habitat selection surface, so the minimum is 1.


Show code
N_CONV_LAYERS_HAB = 8

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
OUTPUT_CHANNELS
Number of convolutional filters (and therefore feature maps) for each convolution layer. More convolutional filters can provide more flexible functions, but will increase the number of parameters and slow down training times.


Show code
OUTPUT_CHANNELS = 8



Pre-calculate the flattened CNN output size
This value will be the input to the fully-connected layers in the movement subnetwork, and is calculated here so that ModelParams can be set without hard-coding it.
flattened_conv_dim() reproduces exactly what the layers inside ConvJointModel do to the spatial dimensions: * conv (padding=1) keeps the spatial dimension unchanged at each layer * maxpool k=2, s=2 halves the spatial dimension (floor division) at each layer
Because every movement conv layer is paired with a max pooling layer, this size depends on N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE — so it has to be recalculated whenever that (or WINDOW_SIZE, or OUTPUT_CHANNELS) changes. It raises an error if the window is pooled away to nothing, which means too many layers for the window size.


Show code
DENSE_DIM = deepssf.flattened_conv_dim(
    image_dim=WINDOW_SIZE,
    n_conv_layers_move=N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE,
    output_channels=OUTPUT_CHANNELS,
)
print(f"After {N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE}x conv+maxpool: dense_dim_in_all={DENSE_DIM}")


After 4x conv+maxpool: dense_dim_in_all=72

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
filter_steps_by_window()
Removes steps whose straight-line displacement exceeds half the spatial window (WINDOW_SIZE × PIXEL_SIZE / 2 metres). Such steps would place the true next location outside the predicted probability map, causing an index error in the loss function.


Show code
original_data_size = len(step_df)

step_df = deepssf.filter_steps_by_window(
    step_df, window_size=WINDOW_SIZE, pixel_size=PIXEL_SIZE
)

print(f"Initial number of steps: {original_data_size:,}")
print(f"Steps after window filter: {len(step_df):,}")
print(f"Data reduction: {original_data_size - len(step_df):,} ({(original_data_size - len(step_df)) / original_data_size * 100:.1f}%)")

Steps after window filter: 252,964
Data reduction: 4,794 (1.9%)

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
make_dataloaders()
Splits step_df into train / val / test subsets (here 80 / 10 / 10 %) and returns a PyTorch DataLoader for each.
The split is a torch.utils.data.random_split, not a chronological one — each subset is a random sample of steps drawn from across the whole dataset and all 28 individuals. Consecutive steps are highly autocorrelated, so a random split leaks information between train and test and will make the validation numbers below look better than genuine out-of-sample performance. If you want an honest held-out estimate, split step_df yourself (by individual, or by time) and build the DataLoaders from the resulting subsets.

Each DataLoader yields tuples of:

x1 — spatial window tensor (batch × n_spatial_channels × H × W)

One channel per raster band in LAYER_PATHS, cropped around each step’s start pixel.

x2 — scalar covariate tensor (batch × len(SCALAR_COLS))

Raw scalar values; broadcast into spatial maps inside the model.

x3 — previous bearing tensor (batch × 1)

Conditions the movement kernel on the direction of the prior step.

(px2, py2) — pixel indices of the true next location within the window

Used by the loss function to look up the predicted probability at the observed destination.



The layer_paths argument causes the function to re-read the rasters internally, so the DataLoader is independent of the env_layers dict loaded above.


Show code
dl_train, dl_val, dl_test = deepssf.make_dataloaders(
    layer_paths=LAYER_PATHS,
    window_size=WINDOW_SIZE,
    batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,
    train_split=0.8,
    val_split=0.1,
    scalar_cols=SCALAR_COLS,
    df=step_df,
)
print(f"Train batches : {len(dl_train)}")
print(f"Val   batches : {len(dl_val)}")
print(f"Test  batches : {len(dl_test)}")
