# Plot the spatial window "tiles" from the first batch: one row per sample, one
# column per raster band.  The centre pixel is the step's start location and the
# cross marks the true next location that the loss function will look up, so this
# is the quickest way to confirm the crops and targets line up with the rasters.
n_samples = 4  # how many samples from the batch to display
n_channels = 6 # number of spatial channels (bands) in the model input
# n_channels = x1.shape[1] # to show all layers, or set to a smaller number to avoid a huge figure

# Band labels straight from the GeoTIFF metadata, in the channel order the model sees
channel_labels = []
for name, arr in env_layers.items():
    if arr.ndim == 2:
        channel_labels.append(name)
        continue
    with rasterio.open(LAYER_PATHS[name]) as src:
        descs = src.descriptions
    for band in range(arr.shape[0]):
        channel_labels.append(descs[band] if descs and descs[band] else f"{name} b{band + 1}")

n_show = min(n_samples, x1.shape[0])

    n_show, n_chan, figsize=(3.0 * n_chan, 3.0 * n_show), squeeze=False
)

for row in range(n_show):

        ax = axes[row, col]

        # True next step — px2 is the column index, py2 the row index

            )

fig.suptitle(

    "(white + = step start, red × = observed next step)",

)

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
ModelParams
A thin dict-like container (it is a wrapper around something else rather than storing data) that groups all architecture hyper-parameters so they can be passed to ConvJointModel and logged together.
This is where the parameters that are passed to the model are set.


Show code
params = deepssf.ModelParams({
    "batch_size":                BATCH_SIZE,
    "image_dim":                 WINDOW_SIZE,           # spatial window size (pixels)
    "pixel_size":                PIXEL_SIZE,            # metres per pixel
    "dim_in_nonspatial_to_grid": len(SCALAR_COLS),      # scalar cols tiled into window
    "dense_dim_in_nonspatial":   len(SCALAR_COLS),      # scalar inputs to the dense MLP
    "dense_dim_hidden":          128,                   # hidden units in the scalar MLP
    "dense_dim_in_all":          DENSE_DIM,             # flattened CNN output size
    # One channel per raster band (not per layer) + the tiled scalar covariates
    "input_channels":            N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS + len(SCALAR_COLS),
    "output_channels":           OUTPUT_CHANNELS,       # feature maps per conv layer
    "kernel_size":               3,                     # conv kernel spatial size
    "stride":                    1,                     # conv stride (should be kept at 1)
    "kernel_size_mp":            2,                     # max-pool kernel size
    "stride_mp":                 2,                     # max-pool stride 
    "padding":                   1,                     # same-padding preserves spatial dimensions
    "num_movement_params":       12,                    # movement kernel parameters
    "n_conv_layers_hab":         N_CONV_LAYERS_HAB,     # conv layers, habitat branch
    "n_conv_layers_move":        N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE,    # conv+maxpool layers, movement
    "dropout":                   0.0,
    "device":                    DEVICE,
})
print(f"input_channels: {params.input_channels}  (must match x1 channels + len(SCALAR_COLS))")


input_channels: 72  (must match x1 channels + len(SCALAR_COLS))

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
ConvJointModel
The deepSSF model! A joint habitat–movement model with two heads: 1. Habitat head — a small CNN applied to the spatial window (env layers + tiled scalars) that outputs a per-pixel log-suitability map. 2. Movement head — a dense MLP (fully-connected layer) that takes the scalar covariates and the previous bearing, and produces parameters for a parametric movement kernel (a mixture of wrapped distributions centred on the current location).
The two log-probability surfaces are summed pixel-wise to give the joint predicted probability map for the animal’s next step.


Show code
model = deepssf.ConvJointModel(params).to(DEVICE)
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Model parameters : {n_params:,}")


Model parameters : 43,117



Print the model structure


Show code
print(model)


ConvJointModel(
  (scalar_grid_output): Scalar_to_Grid_Block()
  (conv_habitat): Conv2d_block_spatial(
    (conv2d): Sequential(
      (0): Conv2d(72, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (1): ReLU()
      (2): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (3): ReLU()
      (4): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (5): ReLU()
      (6): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (7): ReLU()
      (8): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (9): ReLU()
      (10): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (11): ReLU()
      (12): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (13): ReLU()
      (14): Conv2d(8, 1, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
    )
  )
  (conv_movement): Conv2d_block_toFC(
    (conv2d): Sequential(
      (0): Conv2d(72, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (1): ReLU()
      (2): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
      (3): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (4): ReLU()
      (5): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
      (6): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (7): ReLU()
      (8): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
      (9): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (10): ReLU()
      (11): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
      (12): Flatten(start_dim=1, end_dim=-1)
    )
  )
  (fcn_movement_all): FCN_block_all_movement(
    (ffn): Sequential(
      (0): Linear(in_features=72, out_features=128, bias=True)
      (1): Dropout(p=0.0, inplace=False)
      (2): ReLU()
      (3): Linear(in_features=128, out_features=128, bias=True)
      (4): Dropout(p=0.0, inplace=False)
      (5): ReLU()
      (6): Linear(in_features=128, out_features=12, bias=True)
    )
  )
  (movement_grid_output): Params_to_Grid_Block_ChV()
)

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
negativeLogLikeLoss
Scores each predicted probability map against the true next-step pixel index; minimising it pushes probability mass toward observed locations.


Show code
loss_fn = deepssf.negativeLogLikeLoss(reduction="mean")

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
make_optimisers()
Creates two Adam optimisers with separate learning rates:

lr_habitat

controls the CNN (habitat) head

lr_movement

controls the movement branch (conv_movement + fcn_movement_all), kept lower for stability


It also returns a ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler for each optimiser that reduces the learning rate by a factor of scheduler_factor (default = 0.1) if that head’s validation loss does not improve for scheduler_patience epochs (default = 5).
Note that each scheduler now watches its own component of the validation loss. Previously both watched the combined loss, which is dominated by the movement component — so the movement head’s plateau was what cut the habitat learning rate. With that fixed, the two learning rates no longer have to be separated by two orders of magnitude to stop movement from running away with training; start closer together and tune from there.


Show code
optimisers, schedulers = deepssf.make_optimisers(
    model, 
    lr_habitat=5e-5, 
    lr_movement=1e-5, 
    scheduler_patience=3, 
    scheduler_factor=0.5
)

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
EarlyStopping()
Defines when the model should stop training.

patience

If the loss doesn’t improve for patience epochs, terminate training




Show code
early_stop = deepssf.EarlyStopping(
    patience=10,
    verbose=True,
    monitor="both",                 # stop only when BOTH heads have plateaued
    path=str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model.pt"),
    checkpoint_on="active",         # a habitat-only stage saves on habitat loss
    # Also keep each head's own best epoch, across the whole run
    head_paths={
        "habitat":  str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_habitat.pt"),
        "movement": str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_movement.pt"),
    },
)

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
create_gif()
Assembles the snapshots in snapshot_dir into an animation so you can see how the predictions evolve as training progresses.
Display it with IPython.display.Image, which reads the file and embeds the bytes in the notebook’s output. A hand-written <img src="outputs/....gif"> tag does not work here: the notebook’s HTML output is rendered in a sandboxed webview whose base URL is not the notebook’s directory, so a relative path resolves to nothing and you get an empty box. Nothing is generating a still frame — there is simply no image being loaded at all. Embedding also means the animation survives being exported to HTML or shared as a standalone .ipynb.


Show code
gif_path = str(OUTPUT_DIR / "training_progress.gif")
deepssf.create_gif(str(SNAPSHOT_DIR), gif_path, fps=5)
print(f"Training GIF → {gif_path}")

# Embed the GIF's bytes in an <img> tag so it renders wherever the notebook is
# opened.  Image() would do the same, but its image/gif output is one Quarto
# doesn't render (it falls back to the text repr); HTML is passed through as-is.
gif_b64 = base64.b64encode(Path(gif_path).read_bytes()).decode()
HTML(f'<img src="data:image/gif;base64,{gif_b64}" style="max-width:100%">')

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
Training - loss across epochs


Show code
# Three panels rather than one: the habitat and movement components move on very
# different scales, so sharing an axis would flatten the habitat curve into a
# horizontal line.  x = 0 is the pre-training baseline recorded by fit().
uniform_nll = np.log(WINDOW_SIZE ** 2)
epochs = np.arange(len(history["val_losses"]))
stages = np.asarray(history["stage"])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.6), constrained_layout=True)

panels = [
    ("Combined", history["val_losses"], history["train_losses"]),
    ("Habitat", history["val_habitat_losses"], None),
    ("Movement", history["val_movement_losses"], None),
]

for ax, (title, val, train) in zip(axes, panels):
    if train is not None:
        ax.plot(epochs, train, color="0.6", lw=1.5, label="train")
    ax.plot(epochs, val, color="C0", lw=1.5, label="val")
    if title == "Habitat":
        # A uniform surface over the window scores log(H*W), so this line is the
        # "learned nothing" mark — the whole question for the habitat head is how
        # far below it the curve gets.  Movement sits far below it from the first
        # epoch, and drawing it there would only compress that panel's axis.
        ax.axhline(uniform_nll, color="0.4", ls="--", lw=1,
                   label=f"uniform ({uniform_nll:.2f})")
    # Shade the staged-training blocks so the schedule is readable off the curve.
    for s in np.unique(stages[stages >= 0])[1::2]:
        within = epochs[stages == s]
        ax.axvspan(within.min() - 0.5, within.max() + 0.5, color="0.92", zorder=0)
    ax.set_xlabel("Epoch (0 = untrained baseline)")
    ax.set_ylabel("NLL (nats)")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

fig.suptitle("Training history — combined loss and its two components")
plt.savefig(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "loss_history.png"), dpi=100)
plt.show()

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
Choosing which checkpoint to use
fit() leaves the model holding its final-epoch weights, not the best ones, so load a checkpoint before testing or simulating.

best_model.pt — the model to use for simulation. Both heads from one epoch, so the joint likelihood is the one that was actually measured.
best_model_habitat.pt / best_model_movement.pt — each head at its own best epoch, tracked across the whole run.

Mixing them is a deliberate trade: taking the habitat head from a different epoch gives the sharpest habitat surface to map, but the two heads then come from different epochs and the joint model’s likelihood is no longer what either checkpoint recorded. Use it for the landscape predictions below, not for simulating trajectories.


Show code
# The joint model — what the simulations further down should use
ckpt = deepssf.load_checkpoint(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model.pt"), model)
print(f"best_model.pt         saved on '{ckpt['checkpoint_criterion']}' "
      f"= {ckpt['checkpoint_score']:.6f}")

hab_ckpt = deepssf.load_checkpoint(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_habitat.pt"))
print(f"best_model_habitat.pt  saved on '{hab_ckpt['checkpoint_criterion']}' "
      f"= {hab_ckpt['checkpoint_score']:.6f}")

# How much habitat was left on the table by the last epoch.  The two numbers
# above are different quantities (a combined loss and a habitat loss) and are
# not comparable directly, so read the gap off the history instead.
hab_hist = np.asarray(history["val_habitat_losses"])
best_epoch = int(np.nanargmin(hab_hist))
print(f"\nhabitat NLL: best {hab_hist[best_epoch]:.4f} at epoch {best_epoch}, "
      f"final {hab_hist[-1]:.4f} — a gap of {hab_hist[-1] - hab_hist[best_epoch]:+.4f} nats")
print(f"(a uniform surface over the window scores {np.log(WINDOW_SIZE ** 2):.4f} - "
      f"a gap of {hab_hist[-1] - np.log(WINDOW_SIZE ** 2):+.4f}.")

# To map the sharpest habitat surface instead, overwrite just that head:
# load_head_weights(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_habitat.pt"), model, "habitat")

title: deepSSF Model Training
section: Convert the NumPy rasters loaded earlier into PyTorch tensors.
text:
Convert the NumPy rasters loaded earlier into PyTorch tensors.
Both validate_next_step_probs() and simulate_trajectory() call get_landscape(month_index) at each step to fetch the current environmental layers as a list of 2-D tensors.
With static (non-seasonal) rasters the month_index argument is unused. For seasonal data (e.g. monthly NDVI composites) you would index into a stack of layers here based on the current month.


Show code
# validate_next_step_probs() and simulate_trajectory() both stack the list returned
# by get_landscape() along a new channel dimension, so every element must be a *2-D*
# tensor.  Unbind the band dimension of any multi-band layer so the channel order
# matches what MovementDataset fed the model during training.
landscape_tensors = []
for arr in env_layers.values():
    t = torch.from_numpy(np.asarray(arr).astype(np.float32))
    landscape_tensors.extend([t] if t.ndim == 2 else list(t))

print(f"Landscape channels: {len(landscape_tensors)}  (each {tuple(landscape_tensors[0].shape)})")

def get_landscape(_month_index):
    # Returns one 2-D tensor per spatial channel, in the same order as LAYER_PATHS.
    return landscape_tensors

# Take the last 10 % of steps as a test sample.  CAVEAT: make_dataloaders() uses a
# random_split, so these steps were mostly *seen during training* — the numbers below
# are not a clean out-of-sample estimate.  Because step_df is ordered by individual
# name, this slice is also just the last few pigs alphabetically rather than the
# latest steps in time.  Hold out individuals or a date range explicitly for a real test.
n_test      = int(len(step_df) * 0.1)
test_sample = step_df.iloc[-n_test:].reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Testing on {len(test_sample):,} steps")


Landscape channels: 67  (each (1329, 1692))
Testing on 25,296 steps

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
validate_next_step_probs()
Runs the model forward on each test step and records the probability mass assigned to the true next location.

Inputs:

model
test_sample

test dataframe that contains movement steps (from the data loaded above)

get_landscape

retrieves the landscape layers (spatial covariates) that were used to train the model

transform

raster Affine transform

window_size

window size of the local availability window (should be the same as for training)

scalar_cols

scalar column names (should be set from above)

yday_col

which column has the yday column to ensure the correct spatial layers (if dynamic through time) are indexed

month_index_fn

a function mapping day-of-year → month index (used by the get_landscape function). Here we are using static spatial layers so we can set it to 0.


Outputs:

test_sample dataframe with three new columns appended:

habitat_prob — probability at the true location from the habitat head alone
move_prob — probability at the true location from the movement head alone
next_step_prob — joint (habitat × movement) probability at the true location



Higher values mean the model performed better (there was higher predicted probability at the observed next-step).


Show code
# Use the last 10 % of steps as the test set (matches the DataLoader split)
n_test      = int(len(step_df) * 0.1)
test_sample = step_df.iloc[-n_test:].reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Validating on {len(test_sample):,} steps")

val_results = deepssf.validate_next_step_probs(
    model,
    test_sample,
    get_landscape=get_landscape,
    transform=raster_transform,
    window_size=WINDOW_SIZE,
    scalar_cols=tuple(SCALAR_COLS),
    yday_col="yday_t1",
    bearing_col="bearing_tm1",
    month_index_fn=lambda _yday: 0,   # static layers — month doesn't matter
)
print(val_results[["habitat_prob", "move_prob", "next_step_prob"]].describe())

text:
Daily distance travelled


Show code
start_date <- min(pig_all_steps$date)
bin_width <- 3 # days

# daily distance travelled for each pig
daily_distance_id <- pig_all_steps %>%
  group_by(name, date) %>%
  summarise(
    sum_sl = sum(sl_, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# get the rolling mean of the daily distance travelled for each pig
daily_distance_id_rolling_mean <- daily_distance_id %>%
  mutate(
    bin_num  = as.numeric(date - start_date) %/% bin_width,
    date_bin = start_date + bin_num * bin_width + (bin_width-1)/2      # +2 = bin midpoint (5 days: 0-4)
  ) %>%
  group_by(name, date_bin) %>%
  summarise(
    id_sum_sl = mean(sum_sl, na.rm = TRUE),
    q25 = quantile(sum_sl, probs = 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q50 = quantile(sum_sl, probs = 0.5,  na.rm = TRUE),
    q75 = quantile(sum_sl, probs = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    n   = sum(!is.na(sum_sl)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# average daily distance travelled across all pigs
daily_distance_all <- daily_distance_id_rolling_mean %>%
  group_by(date_bin) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_sum_sl = mean(id_sum_sl, na.rm = TRUE),
    q25 = quantile(id_sum_sl, probs = 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q50 = quantile(id_sum_sl, probs = 0.5,  na.rm = TRUE),
    q75 = quantile(id_sum_sl, probs = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    n   = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

title: Seasonal space use
text:
Convert to ctmm telemetry object


Show code
# as.telemetry() identifies columns by their Movebank names, so we rename them.
# x1_/y1_ are in GDA94 / GA Lambert (EPSG:3112), so convert to WGS84 lon/lat
pig_data_movebank <- pig_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(x1_), !is.na(y1_), !is.na(t1_)) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x1_", "y1_"), crs = 3112, remove = FALSE) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 4326) %>%
  mutate(location.long = st_coordinates(.)[, 1],
         location.lat  = st_coordinates(.)[, 2]) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(ID = name,
            timestamp = t1_,
            location.long, location.lat,
            month, season) %>%
  as.data.frame()

# returns a list of telemetry objects, one per individual
pig_data_ctmm <- as.telemetry(pig_data_movebank,
                             timezone = "Australia/Darwin",
                             keep = c("month", "season"))

title: Seasonal space use
text:
Nest the telemetry objects
One row per pig, with the telemetry object in a list column. The movement models and home ranges are then added as further list columns.


Show code
pigs_nested <- tibble(name = names(pig_data_ctmm),
                      telemetry = pig_data_ctmm)

pigs_nested

title: Seasonal space use
section: Fit movement models and estimate home ranges
text:
Fit movement models and estimate home ranges
Model selection is slow, so the results are saved and re-loaded if they already exist. Delete the file to re-fit.


Show code
hr_fits_file <- paste0(outputs_dir, "pigs_nested_akde.rds")

if (file.exists(hr_fits_file)) {

  pigs_nested <- readRDS(hr_fits_file)

} else {

  tic()
  pigs_nested <- pigs_nested %>%
    mutate(
      # automated model guesstimate
      guess = map(telemetry, ~ ctmm.guess(.x, interactive = FALSE)),
      # model selection (defaults to pHREML)
      fit = map2(telemetry, guess, ~ ctmm.select(.x, .y)),
      # area-corrected AKDE
      ud = map2(telemetry, fit, ~ akde(.x, .y, weights = TRUE))
    )
  toc()

  saveRDS(pigs_nested, hr_fits_file)
  beep(sound = 2)

}

title: Seasonal space use
section: Summarise the models and home range areas
text:
Summarise the models and home range areas


Show code
pigs_hr_summary <- pigs_nested %>%
  mutate(
    n_locations = map_int(telemetry, nrow),
    model = map_chr(fit, ~ summary(.x)$name),
    DOF_area = map_dbl(ud, ~ summary(.x)$DOF["area"]),
    # 95% home range area and CIs (units are reported in the column name)
    hr_area = map(ud, ~ {
      CI <- summary(.x)$CI
      tibble(units = rownames(CI), low = CI[1, "low"], est = CI[1, "est"], high = CI[1, "high"])
    })
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(name, n_locations, model, DOF_area, hr_area) %>%
  unnest(hr_area)

text:
Convert to sf and save for QGIS
as.sf() returns three polygons per pig for each contour level - the lower CI, the estimate and the upper CI. We extract the 50% (core area) and 95% (home range) contours. Each UD is in ctmm’s own local projection, so they are all transformed to EPSG:3112 to match the rest of the data.


Show code
# home range contours to extract
contour_levels <- c(0.5, 0.95)

pigs_hr_sf <- pigs_nested %>%
  dplyr::select(name, ud) %>%
  # one row per pig per contour level
  crossing(level_ud = contour_levels) %>%
  mutate(hr_sf = map2(ud, level_ud, ~ as.sf(.x, level.UD = .y, level = 0.95) %>%
                        st_transform(crs = 3112))) %>%
  dplyr::select(name, level_ud, hr_sf) %>%
  # as.sf already has a 'name' column (e.g. "Betty 95% est"), so rename it
  mutate(hr_sf = map(hr_sf, ~ rename(.x, contour = name))) %>%
  unnest(hr_sf) %>%
  mutate(ci = word(contour, -1)) %>%
  st_as_sf(crs = 3112)

pigs_hr_sf



  



Show code
# a single GeoPackage with all pigs (filter on 'level_ud' and 'ci' in QGIS)
st_write(pigs_hr_sf, paste0(outputs_dir, "pigs_hr_akde.gpkg"), delete_dsn = TRUE)

title: Seasonal space use
text:
Plot interactively with leaflet
Each contour level is a separate layer that can be toggled in the layers control. The CIs and GPS fixes are hidden by default.


Show code
# reproject to WGS84 (EPSG:4326) for leaflet, and add the contour area
pigs_hr_sf_wgs84 <- pigs_hr_sf %>%
  mutate(area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 1e6) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 4326) %>%
  mutate(popup = paste0("ID: ", name,
                        "<br>Contour: ", level_ud * 100, "% (", ci, ")",
                        "<br>Area: ", round(area_km2, 2), " km<sup>2</sup>"))

hr_50_est <- pigs_hr_sf_wgs84 %>% filter(level_ud == 0.5, ci == "est")
hr_95_est <- pigs_hr_sf_wgs84 %>% filter(level_ud == 0.95, ci == "est")
hr_95_ci <- pigs_hr_sf_wgs84 %>% filter(level_ud == 0.95, ci != "est")

# GPS fixes (x1_/y1_ are in GDA94 / GA Lambert, EPSG:3112)
pig_map_pts <- pig_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(x1_), !is.na(y1_)) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x1_", "y1_"), crs = 3112) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 4326)

pal <- colorFactor(viridisLite::viridis(n_distinct(pigs_hr_sf_wgs84$name), option = "H"),
                   domain = pigs_hr_sf_wgs84$name)

hr_map <- leaflet(options = leafletOptions(preferCanvas = TRUE)) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$Esri.WorldImagery) %>%
  addPolygons(data = hr_95_est,
              color = ~ pal(name), weight = 2, opacity = 1,
              fillColor = ~ pal(name), fillOpacity = 0.15,
              popup = ~ popup,
              highlightOptions = highlightOptions(weight = 4, bringToFront = TRUE),
              group = "95% home range") %>%
  addPolygons(data = hr_50_est,
              color = ~ pal(name), weight = 2, opacity = 1,
              fillColor = ~ pal(name), fillOpacity = 0.35,
              popup = ~ popup,
              highlightOptions = highlightOptions(weight = 4, bringToFront = TRUE),
              group = "50% core area") %>%
  addPolylines(data = hr_95_ci,
               color = ~ pal(name), weight = 1, opacity = 0.8,
               dashArray = "4 4",
               popup = ~ popup,
               group = "95% CIs") %>%
  # WebGL points, as there can be a lot of fixes
  leafgl::addGlPoints(data = pig_map_pts,
                      fillColor = pal(pig_map_pts$name),
                      fillOpacity = 0.75,
                      radius = 4,
                      popup = paste0("ID: ", pig_map_pts$name,
                                     "<br>Time: ", pig_map_pts$t1_),
                      group = "GPS fixes") %>%
  addLegend(position = "bottomright", pal = pal,
            values = pigs_hr_sf_wgs84$name, title = "Pig ID") %>%
  addScaleBar(position = "bottomleft",
              options = scaleBarOptions(imperial = FALSE)) %>%
  addLayersControl(overlayGroups = c("95% home range", "50% core area",
                                     "95% CIs", "GPS fixes"),
                   options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)) %>%
  hideGroup(c("95% CIs", "GPS fixes"))

# save a standalone copy to open in the browser (or share)
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(hr_map, file.path(outputs_dir, "pigs_hr_akde_map.html"),
                        selfcontained = TRUE)

# Embedding the maps inline makes the rendered page (and its _freeze file)
# too large for GitHub, so when rendering, the saved map is shown in an iframe
# instead (_quarto.yml copies outputs/**/*.html into the site). When working
# interactively the map is shown in the viewer as usual.
embed_map <- function(map, filename, height = 600) {
  if (interactive()) return(map)
  htmltools::tags$iframe(src = paste0(outputs_dir, filename),
                         width = "100%", height = height,
                         style = "border: none;")
}

embed_map(hr_map, "pigs_hr_akde_map.html")

Settings

# minimum number of days with fixes for a pig to be included in a season (~3 months)
min_days_season <- 90

# and in a sub-season (~1.5 months)

title: Seasonal space use
text:
Functions
These are used for both the seasons and the sub-seasons.


Show code
# season of each timestamp, labelled by year
season_id <- function(t) {
  m <- month(t)
  y <- year(t)
  case_when(
    m %in% 5:10 ~ paste(y, "dry"),
    m %in% 11:12 ~ paste0(y, "-", sprintf("%02d", (y + 1) %% 100), " wet"),
    m %in% 1:4 ~ paste0(y - 1, "-", sprintf("%02d", y %% 100), " wet")
  )
}

# sub-season of each timestamp, labelled by year
subseason_id <- function(t) {
  m <- month(t)
  y <- year(t)
  case_when(
    m %in% 5:7 ~ paste(y, "early dry"),
    m %in% 8:10 ~ paste(y, "late dry"),
    m %in% 11:12 ~ paste0(y, "-", sprintf("%02d", (y + 1) %% 100), " early wet"),
    m == 1 ~ paste0(y - 1, "-", sprintf("%02d", y %% 100), " early wet"),
    m %in% 2:4 ~ paste(y, "late wet")
  )
}

# split one pig's telemetry object into periods (seasons or sub-seasons).
# Subsetting the telemetry object keeps its projection, so it matches the
# full-period movement model.
split_telemetry <- function(tel, period_fun) {
  t <- with_tz(tel$timestamp, tzone = "Australia/Darwin")
  periods <- period_fun(t)
  tibble(period = unique(periods)) %>%
    mutate(telemetry = map(period, ~ tel[periods == .x, ]),
           start = map_vec(period, ~ min(t[periods == .x])),
           n_fixes = map_int(telemetry, nrow),
           n_days = map_int(period, ~ n_distinct(as_date(t[periods == .x]))))
}

# fit the movement model to one pig-period and estimate the weighted AKDE.
# The guess takes the model type from pig_fit (the full-period model), and its
# parameters as starting values, which are then re-estimated from the period's data
fit_period_akde <- function(tel, pig_fit) {
  guess <- ctmm.guess(tel, CTMM = pig_fit, interactive = FALSE)
  fit <- ctmm.fit(tel, guess, method = "pHREML")
  list(fit = fit, ud = akde(tel, fit, weights = TRUE))
}

# one row per pig per period, with the period's movement model and weighted
# AKDE. This runs in parallel, and the results are saved and re-loaded if they
# already exist (delete the file to re-run).
period_akde <- function(pigs_nested, period_fun, min_days, file) {

  if (file.exists(file)) return(readRDS(file))

  pig_periods <- pigs_nested %>%
    dplyr::select(name, telemetry, pig_fit = fit) %>%
    mutate(periods = map(telemetry, ~ split_telemetry(.x, period_fun))) %>%
    dplyr::select(-telemetry) %>%
    unnest(periods) %>%
    filter(n_days >= min_days)

  tic()
  future::plan(future::multisession, workers = max(1, parallelly::availableCores() - 2))
  results <- furrr::future_map2(
    pig_periods$telemetry, pig_periods$pig_fit,
    # a failed fit returns NULL rather than stopping the whole loop
    possibly(fit_period_akde, otherwise = NULL),
    .options = furrr::furrr_options(seed = TRUE, packages = "ctmm"),
    .progress = TRUE)
  future::plan(future::sequential)
  toc()

  pig_periods <- pig_periods %>%
    mutate(fit = map(results, "fit"),
           ud = map(results, "ud")) %>%
    dplyr::select(-pig_fit)

  # any pig-periods where the fit failed
  failed <- pig_periods %>% filter(map_lgl(ud, is.null))
  if (nrow(failed) > 0) {
    warning("Fit failed for: ", paste(failed$name, failed$period, collapse = ", "))
  }
  pig_periods <- pig_periods %>% filter(!map_lgl(ud, is.null))

  saveRDS(pig_periods, file)
  beep(sound = 2)
  pig_periods
}

# the number of days of each pig in each period, including those that
# are removed for having fewer than min_days
period_days <- function(pigs_nested, period_fun) {
  pigs_nested %>%
    mutate(periods = map(telemetry, ~ split_telemetry(.x, period_fun))) %>%
    dplyr::select(name, periods) %>%
    unnest(periods) %>%
    dplyr::select(name, period, start, n_fixes, n_days)
}

# 50% and 95% contours (with CIs) of each pig-period as sf (in EPSG:3112)
period_contours <- function(pig_periods, levels = contour_levels) {

  # periods ordered by when they start
  period_levels <- pig_periods %>%
    summarise(start = min(start), .by = period) %>%
    arrange(start) %>%
    pull(period)

  pig_periods %>%
    dplyr::select(name, period, ud) %>%
    crossing(level_ud = levels) %>%
    mutate(hr_sf = map2(ud, level_ud, ~ as.sf(.x, level.UD = .y, level = 0.95) %>%
                          st_transform(crs = 3112))) %>%
    dplyr::select(name, period, level_ud, hr_sf) %>%
    # as.sf already has a 'name' column (e.g. "Betty 95% est"), so rename it
    mutate(hr_sf = map(hr_sf, ~ rename(.x, contour = name))) %>%
    unnest(hr_sf) %>%
    st_as_sf(crs = 3112) %>%
    mutate(ci = word(contour, -1),
           period = factor(period, levels = period_levels),
           area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 1e6) %>%
    dplyr::select(name, period, level_ud, ci, area_km2)
}

# area of each pig in each period, with 95% CIs
plot_period_areas <- function(hr_sf, title) {

  areas <- hr_sf %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = ci, values_from = area_km2) %>%
    mutate(level = paste0(level_ud * 100, "%"))

  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.6)

  ggplot(areas, aes(x = period, y = est, colour = name, group = name)) +
    geom_line(position = dodge, alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high),
                  position = dodge, width = 0, alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_point(position = dodge, size = 1) +
    # mean across pigs
    stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = mean, geom = "point",
                 colour = "black", shape = 4, size = 3, stroke = 1) +
    scale_colour_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
    scale_y_continuous(expression("Area (km"^2*")")) +
    facet_wrap(~ level, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
    labs(title = title,
         subtitle = "Weighted AKDE with 95% CIs. Crosses are the mean across pigs",
         x = "") +
    theme_bw()
}

# leaflet map of the contour point estimates, with radio buttons to choose
# the period, showing that period's (thinned) GPS fixes
period_hr_map <- function(hr_sf, pts_sf, title) {

  hr_sf <- hr_sf %>%
    filter(ci == "est") %>%
    st_transform(crs = 4326) %>%
    mutate(popup = paste0("ID: ", name,
                          "<br>Period: ", period,
                          "<br>Contour: ", level_ud * 100, "%",
                          "<br>Area: ", round(area_km2, 2), " km<sup>2</sup>"))

  periods <- levels(droplevels(hr_sf$period))

  # only show the fixes of pig-periods with a home range (i.e. not those
  # removed for having too few days)
  pts_sf <- pts_sf %>%
    semi_join(hr_sf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
                distinct(name, period) %>%
                mutate(period = as.character(period)),
              by = c("name", "period"))

  pal <- colorFactor(viridisLite::viridis(n_distinct(pig_all$name), option = "H"),
                     domain = sort(unique(pig_all$name)))

  m <- leaflet(options = leafletOptions(preferCanvas = TRUE)) %>%
    addProviderTiles(providers$Esri.WorldImagery)

  # each period is a 'base group', so the layers control shows radio buttons
  for (p in periods) {
    m <- m %>%
      addCircleMarkers(data = pts_sf %>% filter(period == p),
                       radius = 2, stroke = FALSE,
                       fillColor = ~ pal(name), fillOpacity = 0.5,
                       group = p) %>%
      addPolygons(data = hr_sf %>% filter(period == p, level_ud == 0.95),
                  color = ~ pal(name), weight = 2, opacity = 1,
                  fillColor = ~ pal(name), fillOpacity = 0.1,
                  popup = ~ popup, group = p) %>%
      addPolygons(data = hr_sf %>% filter(period == p, level_ud == 0.5),
                  color = ~ pal(name), weight = 1.5, opacity = 1,
                  dashArray = "4 4",
                  fillColor = ~ pal(name), fillOpacity = 0.3,
                  popup = ~ popup, group = p)
  }

  m %>%
    addLegend(position = "bottomright", pal = pal,
              values = sort(unique(hr_sf$name)), title = "Pig ID") %>%
    addScaleBar(position = "bottomleft",
                options = scaleBarOptions(imperial = FALSE)) %>%
    addControl(paste0("<b>", title, "</b>"), position = "topleft") %>%
    addLayersControl(baseGroups = periods,
                     options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE))
}

title: Seasonal space use
text:
Settings
Pig-months with only a few days of data (e.g. when the collar was deployed or dropped off part-way through a month) will have artificially small areas, so they are removed.


Show code
# minimum number of days with fixes for a pig-month to be included
min_days <- 20

# contour levels (50% core area and 95% home range)
contour_levels <- c(0.5, 0.95)

# set to a number to only fit the first n pig-months with ctmm (for testing),
# or NA to fit them all
n_test <- NA

title: Seasonal space use
text:
Split the data into pig-months


Show code
pig_monthly <- pig_all %>%
  filter(!is.na(x1_), !is.na(y1_), !is.na(t1_)) %>%
  mutate(year_month = format(t1_, "%Y-%m"),
         month_date = floor_date(as_date(t1_), "month")) %>%
  nest(data = -c(name, year_month, month_date)) %>%
  mutate(n_fixes = map_int(data, nrow),
         n_days = map_int(data, ~ n_distinct(as_date(.x$t1_)))) %>%
  arrange(name, month_date)

# pig-months that are removed
pig_monthly %>% filter(n_days < min_days) %>% dplyr::select(-data)

# number of pig-months for each month
pig_monthly %>% count(month_date)

title: Seasonal space use
text:
Using MCP
Minimum convex polygons from the amt package. The 95% MCP excludes the 5% of fixes furthest from the centroid.


Show code
hr_monthly_mcp_sf <- pig_monthly %>%
  mutate(track = map(data, ~ make_track(.x, x1_, y1_, t1_, crs = 3112)),
         mcp_sf = map(track, ~ hr_mcp(.x, levels = contour_levels) %>%
                        hr_isopleths())) %>%
  dplyr::select(name, year_month, month_date, mcp_sf) %>%
  unnest(mcp_sf) %>%
  st_as_sf(crs = 3112) %>%
  mutate(method = "MCP",
         level_ud = level,
         area_km2 = as.numeric(area) / 1e6) %>%
  dplyr::select(name, year_month, month_date, method, level_ud, area_km2)

hr_monthly_mcp_sf

section: Set random seed and the device for training the model
text:
Set random seed and the device for training the model
If you have a GPU, this is where it will be specified (automatically).


Code
# Reproducibility — fix random seeds so results are the same on every run.
# These matter here: make_dataloaders() uses random_split, so without a seed the
# train/val/test partition changes every run and two training configurations
# cannot be compared.
torch.manual_seed(42)
np.random.seed(42)

# DEVICE is capitalised — module-level constant (set once, never reassigned).
# get_device() returns 'cuda' if a GPU is available, 'mps' on Apple Silicon,
# or 'cpu' otherwise.  All tensors and the model are moved to this device.
DEVICE = get_device()
print(f"Device: {DEVICE}")

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
Set script paths
If you have cloned/forked/downloaded the GitHub repo (https://github.com/swforrest/deepSSF_package) you shouldn’t need to change these, but for your own analyses you will want to set these to point to where your data is and where you want outputs saved.
All-caps names below are module-level constants — set once here and referenced throughout the notebook without being reassigned. Python has no built-in constant keyword, so capitalisation is the community convention (PEP 8) to signal “do not change this value”.


Code
DATA_DIR = Path("data")  # location of the bundled sample data
MAPPING_DIR = Path("mapping")  # location of the landcover mapping files
CSV_PATH = DATA_DIR / "pig_all_steps_covs_subset_20260813.csv"  # GPS tracking data, 28 individuals

# NOTE: 's2' and 's2_dir' are RESERVED keys in load_environmental_layers().
# 's2_dir' triggers the monthly-composite loader (load_s2_data), and a plain
# 's2' entry is skipped by the per-file loop — so a single multi-band GeoTIFF
# must be given any *other* name, otherwise nothing is loaded and the function
# raises "raster_transform could not be set".
LAYER_PATHS = {
    # 3-band Sentinel-2 composite: NDVI, NDWI, NDMI (20 m, EPSG:3112)
    # "s2_indices": str(MAPPING_DIR / "feral_pig_aoi_S2_indices_2025-09-12_to_2026-06-23.tif"),
    # Alternative — all 12 S2 bands (12 spatial channels instead of 3, slower to train):
    # "s2_median": str(MAPPING_DIR / "feral_pig_aoi_S2_median_full_2025-09-12_to_2026-06-23.tif"),
    # AlphaEarth embeddings (2025)
    "alphaearth": str(MAPPING_DIR / "feral_pig_aoi_alphaearth_2025_crop.tif"),
}
OUTPUT_DIR   = Path("outputs")                   # figures and model checkpoints go here
SNAPSHOT_DIR = OUTPUT_DIR / "training_snapshots"  # per-batch prediction-map snapshots
OUTPUT_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
load_environmental_layers()
Reads each GeoTIFF listed in LAYER_PATHS, min–max

Scales every band to [0, 1], and returns:

env_layers — dict mapping layer name → NumPy array: 2-D (H × W) for single-band GeoTIFFs, 3-D (bands × H × W) for multi-band ones, where each band becomes its own model input channel
raster_transform — Affine object that converts pixel (row, col) indices to the projected coordinates (easting, northing) of the raster(s), which should be in the same CRS as the GPS data. This transform is used whenever we need to translate between pixel space and real-world coordinates.


Two things to watch for:

The keys 's2' and 's2_dir' are reserved for the monthly Sentinel-2 composite loader — a single GeoTIFF passed under the name 's2' is silently skipped (see the note in the paths cell above).
The rescaling uses a single global min/max across all bands of a file, and computes (data - lo) / hi rather than (data - lo) / (hi - lo). Our index raster is int16 scaled by 10 000 with ±10 000 fill values, so the loaded values span [0, 2] rather than [0, 1] and the three indices are not individually normalised. That is workable (the CNN can rescale internally) but if it hurts training, pre-scale each band yourself and save as .npy — non-.tif paths in LAYER_PATHS are loaded with np.load(..., mmap_mode='r') and left untouched, though at least one real .tif must remain in the dict so the transform can be set.



Code
env_layers, raster_transform = load_environmental_layers(LAYER_PATHS)
print("Layers loaded:", list(env_layers.keys()))
for name, arr in env_layers.items():
    print(f"  {name}: shape={arr.shape}, min={arr.min():.3f}, max={arr.max():.3f}")

# Each band of a multi-band layer becomes one CNN input channel, so count bands
# (not layers) here and reuse the total when setting ModelParams below.  Deriving
# it means switching rasters in LAYER_PATHS needs no other edits.
N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS = sum(1 if arr.ndim == 2 else arr.shape[0] for arr in env_layers.values())
print(f"Spatial channels: {N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS}")



Plot each spatial covariate with the observed GPS locations overlaid.
This confirms the raster extent covers the animal’s home range and gives a visual sense of the landscape the model will learn from.


Code
# Flatten env_layers into one (2-D array, label) pair per spatial channel so the
# figure adapts to whatever LAYER_PATHS provides (1 layer of 3 bands, 2 layers of
# 1 band, ...).  Band descriptions come from the GeoTIFF metadata where present.
channel_plots = []
for name, arr in env_layers.items():
    if arr.ndim == 2:
        channel_plots.append((arr, name))
        continue
    with rasterio.open(LAYER_PATHS[name]) as src:
        descs = src.descriptions
    for band in range(arr.shape[0]):
        label = descs[band] if descs and descs[band] else f"band {band + 1}"
        channel_plots.append((arr[band], f"{name}: {label}"))

ncol = min(3, len(channel_plots))
nrow = math.ceil(len(channel_plots) / ncol)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrow, ncol, figsize=(5.5 * ncol, 4.6 * nrow), squeeze=False)

for ax, (arr, label) in zip(axes.flat, channel_plots, strict=False):
    rasterio.plot.show(arr, transform=raster_transform, ax=ax, cmap="viridis")
    # Points rather than a connected line: raw_df holds 28 individuals, so a
    # single line would draw spurious jumps between them.
    ax.plot(
        raw_df["x1_"], raw_df["y1_"],
        "r.", alpha=0.3, markersize=0.7, label="GPS fixes",
    )
    ax.set_xlabel("Easting (m, projected)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Northing (m, projected)")
    ax.set_title(label)
    ax.legend(loc="upper right", markerscale=10)

# Blank out any unused panels in the grid
for ax in axes.flat[len(channel_plots):]:
    ax.axis("off")

plt.suptitle("Spatial covariates with observed GPS locations", y=1.01)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "spatial_covariates.png"), dpi=100)
plt.show()

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
prepare_movement_df()
Converts a fixes dataframe (one row per GPS location) into a step dataframe (one row per movement between consecutive fixes).

For each step it computes:

dx, dy — displacement in projected CRS units (metres)
bearing — direction of travel (radians; 0 = north, clockwise positive)
bearing_tm1 — bearing of the previous step, used as a model input so the network can capture directional persistence by estimating a turning angle
dt_hour — time elapsed between consecutive fixes (hours)
hour_t1, yday_t1 — decimal hour-of-day and day-of-year at the step start location
*_sin1 / *_cos1 — sine/cosine encodings of hour and yday (see SCALAR_COLS below)


The trailing underscore on column names (x1_, y1_, t1_, etc.) flags them as “start of step” variables; x2_, y2_, t2_ are the corresponding “end of step” values, following the convention of the amt package (Signer et al. 2019). The last fix for each individual is dropped because no forward step can be formed.


Code
# The CSV is already in amt step format, but prepare_movement_df() expects one row
# per *fix* and rebuilds the steps itself (it also derives bearing, dt_hour and the
# cyclic time encodings the model needs).  Point it at the step-start columns and
# let it re-form the steps from consecutive fixes.
step_df = prepare_movement_df(
    raw_df, 
    id_col="name", 
    time_col="t1_", 
    x_col="x1_", 
    y_col="y1_"
)
n_dropped = len(raw_df) - len(step_df)
print(f"Movement steps : {len(step_df):,}  ({n_dropped} dropped — last per individual)")
step_df.head()

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
SCALAR_COLS
These are non-spatial inputs. For processing with convolutional layers, they are converted into spatial windows (rasters/arrays), and stacked with the truly spatial covariates.
The model receives a fixed-size spatial window centred on each step’s start location. To let the network express time-varying habitat preferences (e.g. different nocturnal vs diurnal use), scalar covariates are tiled into additional channels of the same H × W size, so every pixel “knows” the current time context when habitat suitability is estimated.

hour_t1_sin1 / hour_t1_cos1

Sine and cosine of (2π × hour / 24), encoding time-of-day as a circular variable. The circular encoding means 23:00 and 01:00 are treated as adjacent — a plain hour value would have an artificial discontinuity at midnight.

yday_t1_sin1 / yday_t1_cos1

Same circular encoding for day-of-year (1–365), capturing seasonal variation in habitat use (e.g. dry-season vs wet-season movements).

dt_hour

Elapsed time between consecutive fixes (hours). Because GPS collars do not always fix at a perfectly regular rate, including dt_hour lets the movement kernel rescale expected displacement proportionally to the actual time interval rather than assuming a fixed fix rate. Note: dt_hour must be supplied at simulation time as well, so that simulate_trajectory() produces inputs consistent with training.




Code
SCALAR_COLS = ["hour_t1_sin1",
               "hour_t1_cos1", 
               "yday_t1_sin1", 
               "yday_t1_cos1", 
               "dt_hour"]

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
WINDOW_SIZE
The size of the local availability window in cells/pixels; 101 pixels × 20 m = 2020 m across, i.e. 1010 m from the centre location to the edge


Code
WINDOW_SIZE = 51

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
PIXEL_SIZE
Raster resolution in CRS units (metres here). Read straight off raster_transform rather than typed in: the transform is the authority on the grid the model is trained against, and a hand-entered value that disagrees with it silently mis-scales the movement kernel — which is parameterised in metres — against a grid measured in pixels.


Code
# transform.a is the cell width, transform.e the (negative) cell height
PIXEL_SIZE = abs(raster_transform.a)

if not math.isclose(abs(raster_transform.a), abs(raster_transform.e)):
    raise ValueError(
        f"Non-square pixels ({abs(raster_transform.a)} x {abs(raster_transform.e)}); "
        "the model assumes square cells."
    )
print(f"Pixel size: {PIXEL_SIZE} m  →  window {WINDOW_SIZE} px = "
      f"{WINDOW_SIZE * PIXEL_SIZE:,.0f} m across")

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
BATCH_SIZE
Number of training samples (movement steps) per training mini-batch


Code
BATCH_SIZE  = 512

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE
How many convolutional layers in the movement subnetwork of the model?
Each of the convolution layers has a max pooling layer, so more layers will result in greater dimension reduction that will feed into the fully-connected layer that outputs the movement parameters.


Code
N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE = 3

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
N_CONV_LAYERS_HAB
How many convolutional layers in the habitat selection subnetwork of the model?
These convolution layers do not have max pooling layers, so there is no dimension reduction. More layers will increase the depth of the model and allow for more abstracted features to be identified, but will slow model training/prediction.
This count includes the final convolution layer, which is the one that collapses the feature maps down to the single-channel habitat selection surface, so the minimum is 1.


Code
N_CONV_LAYERS_HAB = 4

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
OUTPUT_CHANNELS
Number of convolutional filters (and therefore feature maps) for each convolution layer. More convolutional filters can provide more flexible functions, but will increase the number of parameters and slow down training times.


Code
OUTPUT_CHANNELS = 8



Pre-calculate the flattened CNN output size
This value will be the input to the fully-connected layers in the movement subnetwork, and is calculated here so that ModelParams can be set without hard-coding it.
flattened_conv_dim() reproduces exactly what the layers inside ConvJointModel do to the spatial dimensions: * conv (padding=1) keeps the spatial dimension unchanged at each layer * maxpool k=2, s=2 halves the spatial dimension (floor division) at each layer
Because every movement conv layer is paired with a max pooling layer, this size depends on N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE — so it has to be recalculated whenever that (or WINDOW_SIZE, or OUTPUT_CHANNELS) changes. It raises an error if the window is pooled away to nothing, which means too many layers for the window size.


Code
DENSE_DIM = flattened_conv_dim(
    image_dim=WINDOW_SIZE,
    n_conv_layers_move=N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE,
    output_channels=OUTPUT_CHANNELS,
)
print(f"After {N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE}x conv+maxpool: dense_dim_in_all={DENSE_DIM}")

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
filter_steps_by_window()
Removes steps whose straight-line displacement exceeds half the spatial window (WINDOW_SIZE × PIXEL_SIZE / 2 metres). Such steps would place the true next location outside the predicted probability map, causing an index error in the loss function.


Code
step_df = filter_steps_by_window(
    step_df, window_size=WINDOW_SIZE, pixel_size=PIXEL_SIZE
)
print(f"Steps after window filter: {len(step_df):,}")

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
make_dataloaders()
Splits step_df into train / val / test subsets (here 80 / 10 / 10 %) and returns a PyTorch DataLoader for each.
The split is a torch.utils.data.random_split, not a chronological one — each subset is a random sample of steps drawn from across the whole dataset and all 28 individuals. Consecutive steps are highly autocorrelated, so a random split leaks information between train and test and will make the validation numbers below look better than genuine out-of-sample performance. If you want an honest held-out estimate, split step_df yourself (by individual, or by time) and build the DataLoaders from the resulting subsets.

Each DataLoader yields tuples of:

x1 — spatial window tensor (batch × n_spatial_channels × H × W)

One channel per raster band in LAYER_PATHS, cropped around each step’s start pixel.

x2 — scalar covariate tensor (batch × len(SCALAR_COLS))

Raw scalar values; broadcast into spatial maps inside the model.

x3 — previous bearing tensor (batch × 1)

Conditions the movement kernel on the direction of the prior step.

(px2, py2) — pixel indices of the true next location within the window

Used by the loss function to look up the predicted probability at the observed destination.



The layer_paths argument causes the function to re-read the rasters internally, so the DataLoader is independent of the env_layers dict loaded above.


Code
dl_train, dl_val, dl_test = make_dataloaders(
    layer_paths=LAYER_PATHS,
    window_size=WINDOW_SIZE,
    batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,
    train_split=0.8,
    val_split=0.1,
    scalar_cols=SCALAR_COLS,
    df=step_df,
)
print(f"Train batches : {len(dl_train)}")
print(f"Val   batches : {len(dl_val)}")
print(f"Test  batches : {len(dl_test)}")



Inspect one batch to verify tensor shapes match ModelParams expectations
x1 has one channel per spatial band (NDVI + NDWI + NDMI = 3 with the index raster). The scalar covariates in x2 are broadcast to full H × W maps inside ConvJointModel and concatenated with x1 there, giving the CNN N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS + len(SCALAR_COLS) = 3 + 5 = 8 input channels total.
The px2 and py2 are the target that the model is trying to predict, and are the pixel values of the next step (with the centre cell being (50, 50))
next(iter(dl_train)) will call the next batch, which are randomly shuffled, so calling the function again will provide different training samples.


Code
x1, x2, x3, (px2, py2), _ = next(iter(dl_train))
print(f"Spatial   x1 : {x1.shape}   (batch × channels × H × W)")
print(f"Scalars   x2 : {x2.shape}   (batch × len(SCALAR_COLS))")
print(f"Bearing   x3 : {x3.shape}   (batch × 1)")
print(f"Next-step px2: {px2[:4].tolist()}  py2: {py2[:4].tolist()}")




Plot the first set of tiles in the batch


Code
# Plot the spatial window "tiles" from the first batch: one row per sample, one
# column per raster band.  The centre pixel is the step's start location and the
# cross marks the true next location that the loss function will look up, so this
# is the quickest way to confirm the crops and targets line up with the rasters.
N_SHOW = 4  # how many samples from the batch to display

# Band labels straight from the GeoTIFF metadata, in the channel order the model sees
channel_labels = []
for name, arr in env_layers.items():
    if arr.ndim == 2:
        channel_labels.append(name)
        continue
    with rasterio.open(LAYER_PATHS[name]) as src:
        descs = src.descriptions
    for band in range(arr.shape[0]):
        channel_labels.append(descs[band] if descs and descs[band] else f"{name} b{band + 1}")

n_show = min(N_SHOW, x1.shape[0])
n_chan = x1.shape[1]
centre = WINDOW_SIZE // 2

fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    n_show, n_chan, figsize=(3.0 * n_chan, 3.0 * n_show), squeeze=False
)

for row in range(n_show):
    for col in range(n_chan):
        ax = axes[row, col]
        tile = x1[row, col].numpy()
        ax.imshow(tile, cmap="viridis", origin="upper")
        # Start location: always the centre cell of the window by construction
        ax.plot(centre, centre, "w+", markersize=9, markeredgewidth=1.5)
        # True next step — px2 is the column index, py2 the row index
        ax.plot(px2[row].item(), py2[row].item(), "rx", markersize=9, markeredgewidth=1.5)
        ax.set_xticks([])
        ax.set_yticks([])
        if row == 0:
            ax.set_title(channel_labels[col], fontsize=10)
        if col == 0:
            ax.set_ylabel(
                f"sample {row}\n→ ({px2[row].item()}, {py2[row].item()})", fontsize=8
            )

fig.suptitle(
    f"First batch: {WINDOW_SIZE}×{WINDOW_SIZE} tiles  "
    "(white + = step start, red × = observed next step)",
    y=1.0,
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "batch_tiles.png"), dpi=100, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
ModelParams
A thin dict-like container (it is a wrapper around something else rather than storing data) that groups all architecture hyper-parameters so they can be passed to ConvJointModel and logged together.
This is where the parameters that are passed to the model are set.


Code
params = ModelParams({
    "batch_size":                BATCH_SIZE,
    "image_dim":                 WINDOW_SIZE,           # spatial window size (pixels)
    "pixel_size":                PIXEL_SIZE,            # metres per pixel
    "dim_in_nonspatial_to_grid": len(SCALAR_COLS),      # scalar cols tiled into window
    "dense_dim_in_nonspatial":   len(SCALAR_COLS),      # scalar inputs to the dense MLP
    "dense_dim_hidden":          64,                    # hidden units in the scalar MLP
    "dense_dim_in_all":          DENSE_DIM,             # flattened CNN output size
    # One channel per raster band (not per layer) + the tiled scalar covariates
    "input_channels":            N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS + len(SCALAR_COLS),
    "output_channels":           OUTPUT_CHANNELS,       # feature maps per conv layer
    "kernel_size":               3,                     # conv kernel spatial size
    "stride":                    1,
    "kernel_size_mp":            2,                     # max-pool kernel size
    "stride_mp":                 2,
    "padding":                   1,                     # same-padding preserves spatial
    "num_movement_params":       12,                    # movement kernel parameters
    "n_conv_layers_hab":         N_CONV_LAYERS_HAB,     # conv layers, habitat branch
    "n_conv_layers_move":        N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE,    # conv+maxpool layers, movement
    "dropout":                   0.0,
    "device":                    DEVICE,
})
print(f"input_channels: {params.input_channels}  (must match x1 channels + len(SCALAR_COLS))")

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
ConvJointModel
The deepSSF model! A joint habitat–movement model with two heads: 1. Habitat head — a small CNN applied to the spatial window (env layers + tiled scalars) that outputs a per-pixel log-suitability map. 2. Movement head — a dense MLP (fully-connected layer) that takes the scalar covariates and the previous bearing, and produces parameters for a parametric movement kernel (a mixture of wrapped distributions centred on the current location).
The two log-probability surfaces are summed pixel-wise to give the joint predicted probability map for the animal’s next step.


Code
model = ConvJointModel(params).to(DEVICE)
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Model parameters : {n_params:,}")

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
negativeLogLikeLoss
Scores each predicted probability map against the true next-step pixel index; minimising it pushes probability mass toward observed locations.


Code
loss_fn = negativeLogLikeLoss(reduction="mean")

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
make_optimisers()
Creates two Adam optimisers with separate learning rates:

lr_habitat

controls the CNN (habitat) head

lr_movement

controls the movement branch (conv_movement + fcn_movement_all), kept lower for stability


It also returns a ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler for each optimiser that reduces the learning rate by a factor of scheduler_factor (default = 0.1) if that head’s validation loss does not improve for scheduler_patience epochs (default = 5).
Note that each scheduler now watches its own component of the validation loss. Previously both watched the combined loss, which is dominated by the movement component — so the movement head’s plateau was what cut the habitat learning rate. With that fixed, the two learning rates no longer have to be separated by two orders of magnitude to stop movement from running away with training; start closer together and tune from there.


Code
optimisers, schedulers = make_optimisers(
    model, lr_habitat=1e-4, lr_movement=1e-5, scheduler_patience=3, scheduler_factor=0.5
)

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
EarlyStopping
Monitors validation loss and saves the best model weights to disk whenever a new minimum is reached. Training stops automatically if the loss does not improve for patience consecutive epochs.

monitor="both" — when to stop
The combined loss is habitat + movement + logZ, and because the movement surface is sharply peaked on the central pixels (animals mostly stay put between steps) it improves by far more over a run than the diffuse habitat surface does — roughly 1.2 nats against 0.05. Habitat’s improvement therefore sits inside movement’s epoch-to-epoch noise, and monitoring the combined loss alone ends the run on movement’s schedule while habitat is still learning. With monitor="both" each component keeps its own patience budget and training stops only once both have plateaued.


checkpoint_on — when to save
logZ = logsumexp(habitat + movement) is the normaliser of the joint surface. Both surfaces arrive already normalised over the window, so it is the log of
Z = sum over cells of  p_habitat(cell) * p_movement(cell)
— the overlap between the two, i.e. the average habitat probability weighted by where the movement kernel says the animal could actually go. A flat habitat surface gives Z = 1/(H*W), hence logZ = -log(H*W) = -8.64 for a 75 px window — which is why an untrained model reports total ≈ movement almost exactly: the uniform habitat term and the normaliser cancel.
logZ is what makes this a step selection likelihood rather than a plain habitat model. But it also means the combined loss is not monotone in the habitat loss. In the habitat-only stage of the run below, movement is pinned and yet:



epoch
combined
habitat
movement

…

The combined loss falls every epoch, so a checkpoint is written every epoch — but habitat was at its best back at epoch 12 and is getting worse.

Why, given the filters apply the same operation everywhere?
They do — conv_habitat is four Conv2d layers with no positional input (the scalar covariates are broadcast to constant layers), so it is translation-equivariant: identical covariates get an identical value wherever they sit in the window. It cannot single out “near the pig”.
What differs is the availability set each criterion contrasts the used cell against. Writing p_habitat = softmax(f), the habitat gradients are
combined :  E_q[df/dθ]        - df(y)/dθ      q = p_habitat * p_movement / Z
habitat  :  E_p_habitat[df/dθ] - df(y)/dθ
Both raise f at the observed cell and lower it at cells drawn from an availability distribution — pure operations in covariate space. Only the distribution differs:

5460
